paragraphs.text: The words of the Ecclesiastes, son of David, king of Israel in Jerusalem. "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity," said the Ecclesiastes. "What advantage does a man have in all his toil at which he toils under the sun? A generation goes, and a generation comes, and the earth stands for ever. And the sun rises, and draws back to its place. Rising there, it goes toward the south and circles round toward the north. Round and round goes the wind, and on its circuits the wind returns. All the torrents run into the sea, and the sea is not filled. To the place where the torrents go, there they return to go again. All

words are wearisome; a man will not be able to speak. The eye will not be satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing. What is it that has been? The very thing that will be. And what is it that has been done? The very thing that will be done. And there is nothing fresh under the sun. Who will speak and say, 'Look, this is new'? It has already been in the ages that were before us. There is no remembrance of the first things, nor indeed of the last that come to be; there will be no remembrance of them among those who come at the last."

The Ecclesiastes is set before us for interpretation, and the labor of contemplating it is equal to the greatness of its benefit. Once the ideas of Proverbs have trained the mind in advance (its dark sayings and wise utterances, its riddles and intricate turns of speech, as the preface of that book describes), then those who have grown toward the more perfect lessons make the ascent to this Scripture, so lofty and divinely inspired. If, then, Proverbs, the exercise that prepares us for these lessons, is so laborious and so hard to contemplate, how much labor must we expect to find in these lofty thoughts now set before us for contemplation? Those who have worked hard at wrestling under a trainer strip for greater sweat and toil in the athletic contests. In the same way, it seems to me, the teaching of Proverbs is a kind of exercise that trains our souls and softens them up beforehand for the contests of the Church. If, then, the exercise is achieved with so much sweat and toil, what must we reckon of the contests themselves? Or rather, what hyperbole could anyone devise that would express worthily in words how much toil the stadium of this Scripture holds out to those who contend, through athletic experience, for a secure grip on intelligible things, so that the argument is never shown to fall, but the mind is kept upright by the truth in every grapple with the thought? Nevertheless, since this too is one of the Lord's commands, that we must search the Scriptures, it is absolutely necessary to carry it out with as much zeal for the text as we are able. Even if our mind is found to lag behind the truth and fails to reach the greatness of the thoughts, we must still do so, so as not to seem to neglect the Lord's commandment. Let us, then, search the Scripture before us as best we can. For he who gave the command to search will surely also give the power for this very thing, as it is written: "The Lord will give a word to those who preach the good news with great power." And first let the title of the book be set before us for contemplation. In every church Moses and the law are read; the prophets, the psalms, all the history, and whatever belongs to the Old and the New Testament are proclaimed in the churches. How is it, then, that this book alone is singularly adorned with the title "Ecclesiastes"? What

then is our understanding of this? It is that in all the other Scriptures, histories and prophecies alike, the aim looks also to certain other things that are not particularly useful to the Church. What does it matter to the Church to learn in precise detail the disasters of wars, or who became rulers of nations and founders of cities, and who were colonists from where, or what kingdoms would arise in later times, and how many marriages and births of children have been carefully recorded? All such things as each Scripture has to teach, how much could they contribute to the Church's aim of piety? But the teaching of this book looks solely to the way of life of the Church, setting out the means by which one may achieve the virtuous life. For the aim of what is said here is to lift the mind above sense perception, to make it leave behind and cease from everything that appears great and splendid among the things that exist, and through the soul to peer beyond to what sensory apprehension cannot reach, and to acquire a desire for those things that the senses do not attain. Perhaps the title also points to the leader of the Church. For who could the true Ecclesiastes be, who gathers what was scattered into one fullness and calls together into one assembly those who have wandered in many directions through various deceptions, if not the true King of Israel, the Son of God, to whom Nathanael said, "You are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel"? If, then, these are the words of the King of Israel, and this same one is also the Son of God, as the Gospel says, then the same one is also named Ecclesiastes. Perhaps it is not unreasonable for us to refer the meaning of the title to this sense, so that we may learn from it that the force of these words refers to him who founded the Church through the Gospel. "The words," it says, "of the Ecclesiastes, son of David." And so Matthew, at the beginning of his Gospel, names him, calling the Lord the son of David. "Vanity of vanities," said the Ecclesiastes, "all is vanity." "Vain" is understood as what lacks substance, what exists only in the pronouncing of the word. No substantial thing is indicated along with the meaning of the name. It is an idle and empty noise in the form of a word, uttered at random through syllables, striking the ear without meaning, like the words people make up in play, which signify nothing. This is one kind of vanity. Another kind called vanity is the uselessness of things done with effort but toward no goal, as the

[?] seeing, and pursuing with zeal one of the things before him as if it were profitable, he does each thing, and then something contrary happens and his labor comes to nothing. Then the word "vain" signifies that his effort has advanced to no achievement. For in such cases ordinary speech says, "I labored in vain, I hoped in vain, I endured many toils for a vain thing." So that we need not go through every case in which the name "vanity" is properly used, let us sum up the meaning of this word briefly. Vanity is a word without meaning, or a thing without profit, or a plan without substance, or an effort with no end, or in general whatever has no existence for any useful purpose. Now that we understand the meaning of "vain," we should examine what "vanity of vanities" means. Perhaps the idea we are seeking would become clearer if we examined how Scripture usually speaks of things understood in a better sense. Scripture calls the doing of necessary and useful things "work"; but what surpasses other pursuits, whatever looks to the very worship of God, it calls "works of works," as the history shows. By this, I think, the text shows us through a kind of analogy, from the "work of works," what is more to be preferred among our pursuits. For as diligence in work stands to complete idleness, so activity directed to the loftier and more preferable pursuits stands to the other works. In the same way, Scripture speaks of something "holy," and again of the "holy of holies": as the holy surpasses the [?] in holiness by a certain measure, so by the same measure the holy of holies surpasses the holy, being regarded as superlative in sanctity. What we have learned in the better sense, then (that scriptural usage signifies by this kind of expression the intensifying of the underlying idea), we may apply without error to "vanity of vanities." For he says that the things appearing among beings are not simply vain, but are so in a superlative degree of what "vain" means. It is as if someone were to say "deader than the dead" or "more lifeless than the lifeless." Comparative intensification has no place with such words, yet this expression is used to make clear the extreme degree of what is meant. Just as there are things understood as "works of works" and "holies of holies," which are interpreted as superlative indications of the better, so also "vanity of vanities" shows the unsurpassable extreme of vanity. Let no one suppose that these words are an accusation against creation. For if all things were vanity, the charge would pass over to the Maker of all, since he who brought all things into being from nothing would be shown to be the craftsman of these things. But the constitution of man is twofold, soul joined to body, and divided

correspondingly between the two elements we see in ourselves is the form of life as well. The life of the soul is one thing, and the life of the body another. The one is mortal and perishable, the other impassible and incorruptible. The one looks only to the present, while the aim of the other extends to eternity. Since there is a great difference between the mortal and the immortal, between the transient and the eternal, the voice of the Ecclesiastes leads to this: that we should not look to this sensible life, which, compared with the true life, is something without existence or substance. Yet someone might still say that even so the argument does not escape accusing the Creator, since soul and body both come from him. If the life lived through the flesh is accused, and God is the maker of the flesh, such blame must necessarily be referred to him. But this will surely be said only by someone who has not yet gotten outside the flesh, nor peered closely toward the higher life. For whoever has been instructed in the divine mysteries is certainly aware that the life proper and natural to human beings is the life made like the divine nature. The sensory life, carried on through the activity of the sense organs, was given to nature for this purpose: that the knowledge of visible things should become the soul's guide to the knowledge of invisible things. As Wisdom says, "From the greatness of the beauty of created things, the Creator of all is seen by analogy." But human folly did not see what is to be marveled at through the visible things; instead it marveled at what it saw. Since the activity of the senses is transient and short-lived, we learn from this lofty utterance that whoever looks to these things sees nothing. But whoever is led through them to understand what truly is, and through passing things has understood the stable nature and come to comprehend what is always the same, has seen the good that truly is, and has acquired what he saw; for to know this good is to possess it. "For what advantage," it says, "does a man have in all his toil at which he toils under the sun?" He called life in the body "toil," an effort spent for gain that achieves nothing. "For what advantage," he says, "does a man have?" That is, what does the soul gain through the toil of life for those who [live] for what is visible? In what does such life consist? What among the beautiful things we see remains the same? The sun goes round its own course, shining and darkening in turn. It lights the air above us when it shows itself above the earth, and draws darkness after it as it sets. The earth stands still and remains in its fixed immobility [?]; what stands does not move, and what moves does not stand. All things show themselves for what they are throughout every span of time, in no way altered by any change toward novelty. The sea is a receptacle for waters flowing in from everywhere, and

the inflow never ceases, yet the sea never grows. What is the aim of this course for the waters, forever filling what is being filled? For what purpose does the sea receive the inflow of waters, while remaining forever unincreased by the addition? He says these things so that, from the very elements in which human life is lived, he may first explain how insubstantial our pursuits are. For suppose this ordered course of the sun has no end, and the alternation of light and darkness admits no rest. Suppose the earth, condemned to stand still, remains immovable in its fixity, and the rivers toil without end, swallowed up by the insatiable nature of the sea, and the sea receives the inflow of waters in vain, taking into its bosom to no increase what pours in continually. If this is how it is with these things, in what can we expect the human condition to consist, since it has its life among them? And why are we surprised that a generation goes and a generation comes, and that this course never fails nature, each new generation of human beings pushing out the one that came before and being pushed out by the one that comes after? What, then, does the word cry out to the Church through these things? This: "O men, look at the universe and understand your own nature. What you see in heaven and earth, what you observe in the sun, what you perceive in the sea, let these interpret your own nature to you." For like the sun, our nature too has a rising and a setting: one road for all, one circle for the journey of life. When we rise through birth, we are drawn back down again to our kindred place. For when our life has set, our light too goes beneath the earth, when the perception by which we apprehend light [?]; and earth is wholly dissolved into what is akin to it. This is a circle that revolves continually through the same things. It is like the course of the sun, he says: rising over the upper part of the earth, it travels through the southern regions, and passing beneath the earth on the opposite side, it goes under the northern part. In this way, circling for ever, it goes round its own course and comes round again. "For it circles," he says, "circling." So too your spirit goes (he names the whole human spirit from one part), running round this circular course through the same things. "For the spirit goes," he says, "and on its circuits the spirit returns." Whoever understands these things will gain no small benefit for his own life. What is brighter than light? What is clearer than its rays? Yet if the sun goes beneath the earth, its light is hidden and its ray vanishes. Let anyone who looks at this pass his life more soberly, despising splendor here below, and learn from what he sees that distinction does not last for ever. The successions of opposites turn quickly, and nothing remains as it is at present: not youth, not beauty,

not the splendor that comes from power. This is for those who live in some good fortune. But those to whom the life of virtue seems laborious should let their soul be trained by the example of the earth to endure hardships. "The earth stands for ever." What is more wearisome than this immovable fixity? Yet its standing stretches out to eternity. But your time of contest is short. Do not be more lifeless than the earth. Do not be more senseless than insensible things, you who have been granted reason and are guided by reason through life. Rather, "continue," as the Apostle says, "in what you have learned and been assured of," with a firm and immovable stance. For this too is one of the divine commands: "Be steadfast and immovable." Let your self-control remain unshaken in you, your faith firm, your love unchanging, and your stand in everything good immovable, so that the earth in you too may stand for ever. But if anyone gapes after greed, and spreading the boundlessness of his desire out like a sea, is insatiable for gains flowing in from every side, let him look at the real sea and be cured of his disease. For the sea does not exceed its own measure with all the countless inflows of water, but remains at the same fullness, as if no water were added to it. In the same way human nature is bounded by its own measures in enjoying what it has. It cannot greedily broaden its capacity for enjoyment along with the abundance of its income; the inflow stops [?], while the capacity for enjoyment is kept within its own limit. If, then, enjoyment cannot increase beyond the measure of nature, why do we draw in streams of income, and never let the surplus overflow in kindness to others? Since, by the account of vanity given us, vanity is either a profitless word or a profitless thing, the text rightly begins from here, so that we should reckon nothing done or said as having substance, if it looks to the aim of life here below. For all human effort occupied with any of the concerns of this life is plainly like children's games in the sand, whose enjoyment of what they build ends together with their effort in building it. For as soon as they stop working, the sand slides back on itself and [leaves] no trace of what they labored over.

Such is human life. Ambition is sand, power is sand, wealth is sand; sand is each of the things eagerly enjoyed through the flesh. Childish souls now waste themselves on these insubstantial things and endure many toils over each of them; but once they leave the place of sand (I mean life in the flesh), then they will recognize how vain their pastime here was. For along with

material life, its enjoyment comes to an end as well, and they take nothing with them except their conscience alone. This, it seems to me, is why the great Ecclesiastes, as though already outside these things and setting foot with naked soul on the immaterial life, said what we too are likely to say one day. When we leave this seashore, where the sand lies that the sea of life spits up, and are parted from all the waves that crash and roar around us, we will bring from that figurative sea only the memory of what we pursued here, and we will say: "Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity, and what advantage does a man have who toils under the sun?" In my view, this is the word of every soul when, stripped of the things here, it moves to the life it hopes for. Either it has achieved something of the higher things in this life, and then, comparing what it has found, it condemns the state it was in and holds the past in dishonor [?]; or, having been passionately attached to matter, it [meets] the unexpected and learns by experience how useless were the things it labored over in life. Then, lamenting, it will utter this cry, as we human beings do out of regret when we recount our follies in our laments: "Vanity of vanities," and the rest. "All words," he says, "are wearisome, and a man will not be able to speak." And yet at first sight nothing seems easier than speaking. What toil is there for someone who says what he wants? The tongue is supple and nimble, shaping itself effortlessly into whatever form of words it wishes. The drawing of breath from the air, which it uses to produce sounds, is unhindered. The cheeks serve it painlessly, and the lips cooperate in pronouncing what is said. What toil, then, does he see in speech? We do not deliver our speech while digging the ground, or rolling stones, or carrying loads on our shoulders, or doing any other laborious work. The thought formed within us is revealed through the voice and becomes speech. Since such speech involves no toil, we must consider what the toiling words are for which "a man will not be able to speak." "Let the elders," it says, "be counted worthy of double honor, especially those who toil in the word." In ordinary usage, an elder is someone who has passed beyond the disorderly age and reached the settled state of old age. So if someone is unstable in his reasoning and disorderly in his life, he is not yet an elder, even if he appears gray-haired; he is still only a "man." Therefore the words that truly are words, those that serve the profit of souls and the good of people, are full of sweat and toil, and demand much labor to become words. "For the farmer who toils must be the first to receive the fruit," says the craftsman of such words, as though "word" should be understood not as a spoken utterance, but as the [?] in deeds

…virtue, set before those who watch as instruction for life, may take the place of words for those being taught. So all such words are wearisome for those who lead others in virtue, since they first achieve in themselves what they teach. This is what it means that one must first share in the fruits which, before all others, we cultivate for ourselves through virtue. Or perhaps the text also explains the weakness of rational nature. For when we have gone beyond the senses, which have been called vanity, and the mind has somehow slipped into the contemplation of invisible things and tries to present to speech what it has grasped, then speech labours greatly through this interpreting voice, which finds no means of making clear what cannot be uttered. We see the sky, we receive the rays of the heavenly lights through our senses, we have set foot on the earth, we draw in air through the mouth, we use water as our nature sees fit, we admit fire to share in our life. Yet if we want to understand anything about these — what each visible thing is in the account of its essence, where it came from, or how it came to exist — “a man will not be able to speak”, even if he happens to surpass others, because all comprehending knowledge is too weak to declare what is beyond reach. But if speaking about these things involves a labour that exceeds the human power and nature of speech, what would one say happens to words about the Word himself, or about the Father of the Word? There all lofty and grand speech is a kind of obscurity and silence, if it is judged against the true meaning of what is sought. Only this can properly be said of it: even if someone stirs up every line of reasoning and leaves out none of the thoughts that befit God, if his utterance is judged against the worth of the subject itself, whatever he says is not speech. For “man will not be able to speak.” Sight does not bring to a halt the contemplation of visible things that arises in the soul through the eyes. Rather, we are always seeing as if we had never yet seen, and we still hold in ignorance what we take in through the senses. Sight cannot pass beyond colour; the measure of its own activity is what appears to it on the surface of things. Therefore, it says, “the eye will not be satisfied with seeing, and the ear will not be filled with hearing.” The power of hearing receives the account of each thing, but it is not in its nature to be filled. For no account will be found that precisely contains within itself what is sought. How, then, will hearing be filled with hearing about the things sought, when there is nothing that can fill it? Then, after these words, he questions himself and answers himself. For he asks, “What is it that has come to be?” “The very thing,” he says, “that will come to be.” “And what is it that

has been made?” “The very thing,” he says, “that will be made.” What, then, does the question mean? Following from what we have learned, we object to him and say: If all these things are vanity, then clearly none of them has come to be, since they do not exist. For what is vain is wholly without existence, and no one would count the non-existent among the things that have come to be. If, then, these things are not, tell us what it is that has come to be, or that remains in being. His answer to the question is brief: Do you want to know what has come to be? Consider what will be, and you will recognize what has come to be. That is to say: Consider, O man, what you will become when you have raised yourself up through virtue — if your soul has been shaped in every respect by good qualities, if you have got free of the stains of vice, if you have washed from your nature all the filth of material defilement — consider what you will become, adorned by such things, and what form you will put on. If you grasp this by reason, you have been taught what came to be at the first: that which was made in the image and likeness of God. “And where is that now,” I shall say to the one who teaches this, “which once came to be and is hoped for again hereafter, but now is not?” But the teacher of lofty things will certainly give us the same answer: the present things have been called vanity precisely because those things are not found among the present. “And what,” he says, “is it that has been made? The very thing that will be made.” Let none of my hearers think it wordiness or idle repetition when he distinguishes between “what has come to be” and “what has been made.” By each of these terms the text shows the difference between soul and flesh. The soul came to be; the body was made. The text does not use this difference of wording for each of the things signified because the terms mean two different things. It does so to allow you to reason fittingly about each: the soul came to be in the beginning as that which, once purified, will appear again hereafter; the body, formed by the hands of God, was made as that which the resurrection will display at the appointed times. For whatever you see it to be after the resurrection, that is surely what it was made at the first, since the resurrection is nothing other than the restoration to the original state. So he adds what follows from this, saying that outside the original there is nothing. “There is nothing new,” he says, “under the sun.” It is as if he said that whatever is not in accordance with the original does not exist at all, but is only thought to exist. For there is nothing new, he says, under the sun, such that anyone could speak up and point to anything that comes about later and say that this is new and truly exists. This is the sense of what has been said. The wording runs like this: “And there is nothing new under the sun of which one will speak and say, ‘Look, this is new.’” And he presses the point in what follows, saying: “If anything has truly come to be, it is what came to be in the ages before us.” For the very

words of Scripture show this sense, which run thus: “It has already come to be in the ages that were before us.” And if forgetfulness of what came to be has prevailed, do not be surprised, for the things that exist now will also be overtaken by forgetfulness. When our nature inclined toward evil, we became forgetful of the good; but when our return to the good comes about again, evil will in turn be covered over by forgetfulness. I think this is the sense of the words in which he says, “There is no memory of the first things, and indeed of the last things that come to be there will be no memory.” It is as if he said: Of the things that came about after our original good fortune, through which humanity fell into evils, the memory will be erased by what comes about at the last. There will be no memory of them alongside the things that come to be at the end; that is, the final state has brought about the complete obliteration from our nature of the memory of evils, in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and power to the ages of ages.

“I,” he says, “the Ecclesiast.” We have learned who the Ecclesiast is: he who gathers into one what had strayed and been scattered, and makes all into one flock, so that none may be out of earshot of the good shepherd’s voice, which gives life to all. “For the words that I speak,” he says, “are spirit and are life.” He calls himself the Ecclesiast, just as he calls himself physician, and life, and resurrection, and light, and way, and door, and truth, and all the names of his love for humankind. The physician’s voice is properly addressed to the sick. The Word of life becomes active among the dead: when they hear the voice of the Son of Man, they no longer remain in their ancient deadness, and those in the tombs long for the voice of the resurrection. The word of light suits those in darkness, the way is smooth for those who have strayed, and the door is for those who need to enter. In the same way the Ecclesiast surely converses with those who assemble as the Church. So the Ecclesiast speaks to us; let us, then, the Church, listen to his words. As a chorus looks to its leader, sailors to the helmsman, and the battle line to the general, so those who make up the fullness of the Church look to the leader of the Church. What, then, does the Ecclesiast say? “I became king over Israel in Jerusalem.” When was this? Surely when “I was established as king by him on Zion, his holy mountain, proclaiming the decree of the Lord”? To him the Lord said, “You are my Son,” and, “Today I have begotten you.” For he said that he had begotten the maker of all things, the father of the ages, “today,” so that by attaching a temporal word to the time of the birth he might indicate not his existence before the ages, but his birth in time through the flesh for the salvation of humankind.

These, then, are the things the true Ecclesiast goes through, teaching, I think, the great mystery of godliness: why God was manifested in the flesh. “For I gave my heart,” he says, “to seek and to examine in wisdom all things that come to be under heaven.” This is the reason for the Lord’s coming to dwell among humans through the flesh: to give his heart to examine, in his own wisdom, the things that come to be under heaven. The things above heaven did not need anyone to visit them, just as what is not in the grip of disease does not need a healer, since the evils are about the earth. That creeping and violent beast, the serpent, dragging itself along on breast and belly, makes the earth its food and feeds on nothing heavenly. Crawling on what is trodden underfoot, it always looks toward what is trodden, watching for the heel of the human traveller and injecting its venom into those who have lost the authority to tread on serpents. This is why he gave his heart to seek and to examine all things that come to be under heaven. For in the realms above the heavens the Prophet sees the divine majesty unhumbled, when he says, “Your majesty is lifted up above the heavens” — since even the heavenly part was humbled through evil; for so the Psalmist says, that they were humbled because of their sins. This is what the Ecclesiast came to examine: what had come to be under heaven that had not existed before; how vanity entered, how the non-existent gained the upper hand, what the dominion of what does not exist consists in. For evil has no substance, since it has its existence from non-being, and what does not exist from Being has no existence at all in its own nature. Yet vanity prevails over those who have made themselves like vanity. So he came to seek out in his own wisdom what had come to be under the sun, what the confusion of affairs here is, how being was enslaved to non-being, how what has no substance lords it over what is. “And he knows that God has given an evil distraction to the sons of men, to be distracted by it.” It is not pious to take this as one might at first glance, as though God himself gave men the evil distraction; for then the cause of evils would be traced back to him. What is good by nature is surely a provider of good things, since every good tree bears good fruit, and grapes do not grow from thorns, nor thorns from a vine. So what is good by nature would not bring out anything evil from its treasures. Not even the good man speaks evil out of the abundance of his heart, but utters what accords with his own nature. How much more, then, would the fountain of good things never pour out anything evil from its own nature! The more pious interpretation proposes that we understand it this way: that the good is God’s gift. And this gift is the free self-determination

which, through humanity’s mistaken use of it, became an instrument of sin. For freedom of choice and being unenslaved is a good thing; no one would count what is subject to necessity among good things. But this self-determining impulse of the mind, flowing away [?] toward the choice of vice, became a distraction for the soul, which was dragged down from lofty and honourable things to the passionate movements of nature. This is what “he gave” signifies: not that God himself put evil into human life, but that man, through his folly, used the good things given by God in the service of evils. It is customary for Holy Scripture to express such thoughts in such language, as in “God gave them up to dishonourable passions,” and, “He gave them up to a debased mind,” and, “He hardened Pharaoh’s heart,” and, “Why, Lord, have you made us stray from your way, and hardened our hearts so that we do not fear you?” and, “He made them wander in a trackless waste, where there is no road,” and, “You deceived me, and I was deceived,” and all similar passages. In these, the precise understanding does not hold that anything [?] has come into human nature from God; rather, it accuses the free power, which is good and a gift of God given to our nature, but which became evil through its inclination toward the opposite. So the Ecclesiast saw all the things that have been made in life under the sun, that all was vanity. “For there was none who understood, there was none who sought God,” since all turned aside and together became worthless. That is why, after saying, “And behold, all is vanity,” he added the cause: that God is not the cause of these things, but the choice of the human impulse, which he called “spirit.” He accuses this spirit, not because it was like this from the beginning — for if it had been made so, it would be beyond accusation — but because, having been perverted, it was put out of harmony with the

[?] “For what is perverted,” he says, “cannot be adorned”; that is, what is perverted could have no place in the creation adorned by God. Consider a craftsman who is building something for himself according to a plan. With rule and line he straightens the parts which, by their skilful relation to one another, together complete the work of the vessel. If any of them is not made straight according to the line, the straight fitting of the whole will certainly not admit the distortion; that part too must be brought to the line and made straight if it is to fit together with what is straight. In the same way, the Ecclesiast says, a nature perverted by vice cannot find a place in the creation ordered by right reason. “And what is lacking,” he says, “cannot be numbered.” Scriptural usage teaches us to understand “to lack” as “to fall short,” and this can be confirmed from

many passages. Paul, who had been initiated into everything and in all circumstances, knows how both to be in want and to abound. The one who squandered his father’s estate through riotous living began to be in want when famine took hold. And Paul, describing the saints, mentions among the other bodily sufferings they endured that they were “in want, afflicted.” So here too, in saying “what is lacking,” the text indicates by the word what is missing; and what is missing cannot be counted among the things that exist. The disciples, as long as they were all in their full complement, numbered twelve; but when the son of perdition perished, the number was cut short, because what was missing was not counted with those who were. After Judas they both were eleven and were called eleven. So, he says, what is lacking cannot be numbered. What does the text signify by this? That once our state too was counted within the whole; for we too helped make up the sacred hundred of rational sheep. But when the one sheep — our nature — strayed from the mountain pasture, dragged down by vice into this salty and parched place, the same number is no longer recorded for the flock of those who did not stray; they are called ninety-nine. For what is vain falls outside the number of things that exist, because what is lacking cannot be numbered. So he came to seek and to save what was lost, and, taking it up on his shoulders, to restore to the things that exist what was perishing in the vanity of the non-existent, so that the number of God’s creation might once again be complete, the lost one being saved and rejoined to those who were not lost. What the return of the one who strayed is, and what the manner of the return from evils to the good, we are taught in what follows. For he who was tested in every respect just as we are, yet without sin, speaks to us from our own condition; he who took up our weaknesses shows us, through those very weaknesses of our nature, the road that leads away from vice. Consider now, I ask you, that Wisdom speaks through Solomon himself according to the flesh, and speaks of those things that would most effectively lead us to look down on what people strive after. For his words do not come to us as those of most people would, who do not have what they desire within their power, so that he would lose credibility by condemning things he had never experienced. We do not learn everything by our own experience; we know only by reasoning those things whose pleasures poverty prevents us from enjoying. And if we give anyone the advice that what people honour should be counted as nothing, the listener’s objection is ready to hand: that we despise those things because we have not come to know them by experience. But when it is this man who discourses to us on these matters, every such objection falls idle. For it is Solomon who says these things; and this Solomon was the third among the kings of

Israel, after the well-known Saul and David, the chosen of the Lord. He received the rule from his father, and once he had grown to the height of power, he was proclaimed king over the Israelites. He no longer wore down his subjects through war and battle, but, with full authority, lived [?] in peace, and made his business not the acquisition of what he lacked but the enjoyment of what he had, since nothing stood in his way in anything he desired. His wealth stretched as far as his desire, his leisure for enjoyment was unrestricted, and nothing unwelcome interrupted his life amid the things he desired. Besides being wise in other respects, and clever enough to invent something for pleasure, he says he devised this and that among the things people pursue for enjoyment. Having done everything that he lists in order in his account, he says he learned by experience itself that the one end of everything pursued in these things is vanity. He arranged his narrative in this order: first, in the early years of his life, he devoted his leisure to education and did not grow slack in the efforts such labours require. He used “the choice of the spirit” — that is, the impulse of nature — for the increase of knowledge, even though his goal was achieved only with toil. And having grown in this way through wisdom, he examined the passionate and irrational deception of humankind concerning bodily pleasures not by reasoning alone, but also came to recognize the vanity of each of the things pursued through experience itself. This is the aim of what has been examined. Now it would be time to set out in order, following the sequence of the text, the contemplation of it word by word. “I spoke in my heart, saying, ‘Behold, I have become great.’” That is: since I saw around me the greatness that came from power, and the weight of the kingdom come upon me all at once — yet before all these things I valued above everything the possession of wisdom, which cannot be acquired except with toil and sweat. That is why, having said, “I spoke in my heart, saying, ‘Behold, I have become great,’” he added, “I added wisdom.” For I increased the weight of power that had come to me of its own accord by adding wisdom to it, telling myself that I must above all be shown superior to the kings before me for this reason, and excel them in wisdom. “For I added wisdom,” he says, “beyond all who were before me in Jerusalem, and I considered how these things might come about.” For who does not know that wisdom consists, for those who love toil, in knowing what others have toiled over before them? “Therefore,” he says, “my heart saw much, wisdom and knowledge” — not as though the knowledge of such things arose of its own accord and without effort. Rather, he says, since I gave my heart to know wisdom and knowledge, I would not have learned those things unless toil and study had led the way to the knowledge of them. “And also parables,” he says.

[?] “…and knowledge I came to know”: that is, the grasp of what lies beyond us, gained by analogy through comparison with things close at hand. He says he has learned these things: “Parables,” he says, “and knowledge I came to know.” In the same way the Lord, teaching his hearers in the Gospel, sets the word about the kingdom before their eyes by telling of a pearl, or a treasure, or a wedding, or a seed, or leaven, or something of the kind. He does not say that the kingdom is these things. Rather, through the likeness of what they signify, he shows his hearers in parables certain glimmers and riddles of realities beyond comprehension. “And this,” he says, “became the choice of my spirit: that I should gain a great store of wisdom,” so that by becoming wise I might not miss the knowledge of the things that are, nor fail to find what is profitable. For knowledge arises from wisdom, and knowledge makes it easier for us to judge what is fitting. But this does not come to those who strive for it without toil. Whoever adds knowledge to himself certainly increases the labour along with the learning. That is why he says, “He who adds knowledge adds pain.” Only after becoming such a man does he condemn pleasures as vain. For he says, “I said in my heart, Come now, I will test you with gladness; and behold, with good things. And this too is vanity.” He did not give himself to this trial at once, nor did he slip into a share of pleasures without first tasting the hard and more austere life. He first trained himself in that life and established in his character the unsmiling and unyielding temper through which, above all, the lessons of wisdom come to those who strive for them. Only then did he let himself down to the things thought delightful to the senses. He was not dragged toward them by passion, but went to examine whether sensing these things contributes anything to the knowledge of what is truly good. So at the outset he makes even laughter his enemy and calls that passion “distraction,” which in meaning is the same as derangement and madness. For what else could one properly call laughter? It is neither a word nor a deed done for any purpose. It is an unseemly loosening of the body, a convulsion of the breath, a shaking of the whole frame, a stretching of the cheeks, a baring of teeth and gums and palate, a bending back of the neck, and an absurd breaking of the voice, chopped up as the breath breaks. What else could this be, he says, but madness? That is why he says, “To laughter I said, Distraction,” as if he were saying to laughter: You are raving and beside yourself. You do not stay within your settled state. You disgrace yourself willingly and distort your appearance in this passion, and the distortion serves no useful purpose. “And to gladness I said, What are you doing?” This is the same as saying: I stood firm against pleasure, suspicious of [?]

its approach, as if it were a thief slipping secretly into the storerooms of the soul. I never let it take control of my mind. As soon as I recognized pleasure creeping like a wild beast around my senses, I at once fought back and resisted it. To this slavish and irrational gladness I said: “What are you doing? Why do you make the manliness of nature effeminate? Why do you slacken the vigour of the mind? Why do you unstring the tone of the soul? Why do you corrupt my reasonings? Why do you [?] the clear, pure sky of pure thoughts with the darkness of your own fog?” After doing these and similar things, he says, “I examined whether my heart would draw my flesh like wine.” That is, he wanted care for intelligible things to prevail over the movements of the flesh, so that nature would not be at war with itself, the mind choosing some things while the flesh pulled toward others. He wanted to make the mind of our flesh obedient and subject to the intellectual part of the soul, the lesser drawn in and swallowed up by the greater, as happens with the thirsty. For when wine is brought to a thirsty mouth it does not stay in the cup. It passes over to the drinker and disappears as it is eagerly drawn inside. When this happened, my path to the knowledge of the things that are became unerring and unhindered. “My heart,” he says, “guided me in wisdom.” Through wisdom I overcame the revolt of the pleasures, and instruction became the means by which I mastered gladness [?]. That is how the sequence of the text runs. What I sought most of all in knowledge was not to spend my life on anything vain, but to find that good which keeps whoever attains it from missing the judgment of what is beneficial. That good lasts and is not temporary. It extends through the whole of life and becomes a hope for good at every age, first, middle and last, and through the whole number of one's days. “Until I see,” he says, “what is the good for the sons of men, which they shall do under the sun for the number of the days of their life.” Things pursued through the flesh may entice the senses ever so strongly for the moment, but their gladness lasts only an instant. Nothing that happens in the body can give lasting pleasure. The pleasure of drinking ends with satiety. So with eating: fullness quenches the appetite. Any other desire likewise withers once it gets what it desires, and if it arises again, it withers again. None of the things that delight the senses lasts forever or stays the same. Besides, one thing is good for infancy, another for the prime of youth, another for one past his prime, another for one past that age, and yet another for the old man already sinking back into the earth. “But I,” he says, “was seeking that good which is equally good for every age and every season of life.” No satiety of it is expected and no fullness is found. Instead, appetite grows along with

participation, longing reaches its height together with enjoyment, and it is not bounded by the age of the one who desires. The more one delights in this good, the more desire stretches out with the delight, and the delight is kindled together with the desire. At every stage of life it is always beautiful to those who pursue it. It does not change with the instability of ages and seasons. It is good to one who shuts his eyes and to one who looks up, to one who prospers and to one who grieves, to one who passes the night and to one who passes the day, and simply to everyone in every circumstance of life. It becomes neither worse nor better through anything that happens to someone by chance, and it neither shrinks nor grows. This, in my view at least, is the truly existing good, which Solomon sought to see, which men would do under the sun through the whole number of their life. It seems to me nothing other than the work of faith. Its working is common to all, set before all who will on equal terms. It is all-powerful and endures throughout life. This is the good work. May it come about in us too, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory to the ages of ages. Amen.

Now it is time to examine what the voice of the Ecclesiast will teach us next. In the first homily we learned what we learned: that he who gathers all creation into an assembly, who seeks the lost and gathers the wanderers into one, is the one who visits earthly life. What lies under heaven is earthly, and the text calls it “under heaven”; in it deceit and what has no real existence hold sway. In the second exposition we learned that the indictment of the pleasure-loving and passionate disposition was made in the person of Solomon. This was so that the rejection of such things would be credible to us, coming from one who had full power to enjoy every pleasure and who spat upon all that people seem to strive for as worth nothing. What, then, do we learn next, on this third occasion? I think it is the lesson best suited of all to those gathered in the assembly. I mean the confession of things done against reason, which produces the feeling of shame in the soul through the disclosure of wrongdoing. The sense of modesty stored up in human beings seems to be a great and strong weapon for escaping sin. I think God implanted it for this very purpose, so that such a disposition of the soul might turn us away from what is worse. Modesty and the feeling of shame are akin and closely related, and both of them hold sin back, if one is willing to use this disposition of the soul for that purpose. Modesty has often trained people to avoid wrongdoing more effectively than fear. And shame, following the exposure of a fault, is enough by itself to bring the sinner to his senses, so that he does not fall into the same things again. If one were to sketch the difference between them by a definition,

one might say that shame is modesty intensified, and modesty, conversely, is shame relaxed. The colour of the face also shows both the difference and the kinship between these feelings. Modesty is marked by a blush alone: the body somehow shares the soul's feeling through a natural disposition, and the heat around the heart boils up to the surface of the face. But someone ashamed at the exposure of his fault turns livid and reddish, because fear has mixed bile with the blush. Such a feeling, then, would be enough to keep those already caught in some wrongdoing from falling into it again, once they have had their exposure in shame. If this is so, and the argument has rightly judged this feeling to be implanted in nature as a guard against faults, then it is right to regard the amendment achieved by confessing one's faults as a lesson proper to the Church. Through it one can fortify one's own soul with the weapon of shame. Consider someone who through unbridled gluttony gathers indigestible humours inside himself. When his body becomes inflamed, he is cured of the disease by the knife and the cautery. Afterwards, when he looks at the scar of the cautery on his body, he has it as a kind of tutor against disorder for the rest of his life. In the same way, whoever has exposed himself publicly by confessing hidden things sets the memory of that shame over the rest of his life as a tutor. These, then, are the things the Church is taught through the present reading from Ecclesiastes. With a free voice he makes it public. As if setting up an inscribed monument before all people, he presents a confession of the things he did, things such that ignorance and silence about them would be more honourable than speaking of them. I cannot say with precision whether he says these things because he really did them, or whether he invents them for our benefit in order to carry the argument through consistently to its goal. In any case, he describes things that someone with his eye on virtue would not willingly take part in. Perhaps, for the sake of the divine plan, he narrates what never happened as though it had, and accuses himself as one who had tried these things, so that we might turn away from desire for what he condemns before we try it ourselves. Or perhaps he willingly let himself down to the enjoyment of such things in order to train his senses through their opposites. Let anyone who wishes direct his conjecture whichever way he likes. But if someone says that he really did engage in the experience of pleasures, we understand it this way. Think of those who dive to the depths of the sea and search the bottom in case they find a pearl or something else that grows in the deep. Their hardship under water brings them no pleasure; the hope of gain is what made them divers. In the same way, if

Solomon was in these things, then surely, like one of those who dive for purple-fish in the sea, he plunged himself into luxury. He did not go in order to be filled with seawater, and by seawater I mean pleasure. He went to seek what in such a depth is useful to the mind. In my judgment at least, what is useful and to be found through such things is one of two. The first is the blunting of the body's impulses by freely setting before it whatever it wants, since nature always strains harder toward what is forbidden. The second is that the teacher enters these things for the sake of credibility. A thing despised by someone who learned its vanity from experience will no longer be thought desirable by others. They say, in fact, that physicians practise their art most successfully in the diseases they have come to know in their own bodies. They become safer advisers and healers in matters they understand from having been treated themselves, because their own suffering taught them first. Let us see, then, what the one who heals our life says he experienced in his own. “I enlarged my work,” he says; “I built houses.” From the start the discourse is an accusation. He does not say “God's work, which I am,” but “I enlarged my own.” My own work is nothing other than what brings pleasure to the senses. Taken generally, this work is one; but divided in detail, the needs of luxury force it to be split into many parts. For whoever has once gone down into the stuff of the deep must turn his eye in every direction from which pleasure might spring up. Water is channelled from one spring in many directions through pipes, and what is divided off from the spring is no less water, even if it flows from countless spouts. In the same way pleasure, though one by nature, seeps out [?] everywhere in different forms through the variety of human pursuits, slipping in along with the needs of life. Life, for example, has made a dwelling necessary for our nature, because human beings are too weak to bear the extremes of heat and cold. Up to this point a house is useful for living. But pleasure has forced man to go beyond the limits of need. As though he were not providing for the needs of the body but devising delights and luxuries for the eyes, he is almost grieved that he could not make the sky itself his roof, or build the sun's rays into his ceiling. So he widens the boundaries of his buildings on every side, making the enclosure of his dwelling into another world for himself. He raises the walls as high as they will go. He decorates the interiors of the rooms with ornaments of every kind. Stone is quarried from Laconia, Thessaly and Carystus. The quarries of the Nile and of Numidia are searched out so that their stone can be cut into slabs with iron. Somewhere along the way even Phrygian stone has been taken up into these pursuits. It scatters a purple dye through the whiteness of its marble to make a blend, and it becomes a luxury for greedier eyes, painting on the white a varied

and many-shaped spread of colour. How much effort goes into these things! How many contrivances, how many machines! Some workers saw the materials with water and iron, others by human hands, toiling night and day at the [?]. And even this was not enough for those labouring over vain adornment. The purity of glass too is stained with chemicals into various colours, so that it too may add something to the luxury of these fancies. How could anyone describe the elaborate ceilings? There the cedar timbers, by the tricks of art, are turned back into what look like trees again, putting out branches, leaves and fruit in their carvings. I say nothing of the gold beaten into thin, airy films and laid over all these surfaces to draw the greedy eyes to itself. And what could one say about the ivory imported for the elaborate ornament of doorways, the gold smeared over its carvings or the silver hammered on with nails, and all such things? Or the floors of the houses gleaming with stones of many colours, so that even their feet may revel in the radiance of the stones? Or the ambition for a multitude of rooms, which no need of life makes necessary, but which desire, advancing by way of folly, invents out of all proportion? There must be rooms for running and others for strolling, some for entering and others for before the entrance, and still others above the gates. The gates, the porches and the open space within the gates are not thought enough for show unless something meets visitors first that strikes them with amazement the moment they enter. Besides these there are baths that compete in this ambition, their use flooded with whole rivers from abundant spouts. In front of them gymnasia are set up, and these too are lavishly adorned with varied marbles. Colonnades all around the dwelling are held up by Numidian or Thessalian or Aeginetan [?] columns. Bronze is shaped into countless forms in statues, wherever the desire for elaboration pours the material. There are marble images, and pictures on panels through which they commit fornication even with their eyes, since art by imitation lays bare what ought not to be seen. And there are all the other things one can see in such places, contrived to astonish and allure. How could anyone go through each of these in words? Such zeal is itself an accusation and proof of neglect toward the things that matter more. The more a man multiplies his zeal for building, in quantity and in rivalry over materials, the more he exposes how unadorned his soul is. For whoever looks to himself and adorns his own true dwelling, so that one day he may receive God to live in it, has other materials from which beauty

[?] is given to such a dwelling. I know of gold that gleams in such works: the gold mined from the thoughts of Scripture. I know of silver: the divine oracles refined by fire, whose brightness flashes out as it shines through truth. If you take the gleam of the varied stones that adorn the walls and floors of such a temple to mean the varied dispositions of the virtues, you will not miss the adornment fitting for the house. Let the floor be paved with self-control, so that the dust of earthly thought will not trouble the one who lives there. Let the hope of heaven beautify the ceiling. Looking up to it with the eye of the soul, you will see not images of beauty shaped by carving, but the archetypal beauty itself. It is not embellished with gold and silver; it is above gold and much precious stone. If we must also sketch in words the ornament of the side walls, let incorruption and freedom from passion be woven into the house on one side, and let righteousness and freedom from anger adorn the dwelling on the other. On another wall let humility and patience shine out, and on yet another, reverence toward the Divine. And let love, the good craftsman, fit all these neatly together. If you desire baths, you have, if you wish, a bath at home and your own spouts, in which you can wash away the stains of the soul. The great David used it too, delighting in such a bath by night. As for columns to hold up the portico of the soul, do not fuss over Phrygian or porphyry ones; let steadfastness and immovability in every good be your [?] of these material ornaments. [?] all kinds of things, whether in paintings or in sculptures, which people contrive deceptively to imitate the truth: such a dwelling does not admit them, since it is full of the statues of truth. If you want running-tracks and walks, you have the way of life in the commandments. For so Wisdom says: “I walk in the ways of righteousness, and I move about in the midst of the paths of justice.” How good it is for the soul to move about and exercise in these, and, having passed through the ground of one commandment, to turn back to the same course again: that is, having fulfilled the commandment it was striving for, to go on again to a second and a third [?]. Let uprightness of character and the decorum of life adorn it. Whoever trains his building toward beauty in this way will care little for earthly materials. He will not trouble the mines. He will not cross Indian seas to trade in elephants' bones. He will not hire the elaborate skills of craftsmen, whose art, attaching itself to matter [?]. Instead he has at home the wealth that supplies such constructions.

To the more kindly disposed of his sons, the indecency seemed worthy of pity; but to the wicked and ill-bred one, the spectacle of drunkenness became an occasion for laughter. The confession about planting vineyards takes in a long list of evils. All that

[?] for whatever passions wine produces, the passage implicitly contains them all. For who in the world does not know that wine, once excess carries it past need, kindles licentiousness, supplies pleasures, ruins youth, disgraces old age and dishonours women? It is a drug of madness, provision for drunken violence, a poison to the soul, a deadening of the mind, an estrangement from virtue. From it comes laughter without pretext, lamentation without cause, tears that flow of their own accord, groundless boasting, shamelessness in lying, desire for things that do not exist, hope for the impossible, overblown threats, irrational fear, insensibility to what is truly fearful, causeless suspicion, unreasonable friendliness, promises of the impossible. And that is to pass over the rest: the unseemly nodding, the slack heaviness of the head, the indecency that comes of immoderate surfeit, the loosening of the joints, the drooping of the neck, which no longer holds itself up on the shoulders because the moisture from the wine loosens the ligament of the neck. What brought about the lawless abomination of a father lying with his daughters? What stole Lot's mind away from what was happening, so that he both dared the abomination and did not know what he had dared? Who invented, as in a riddle, the strange naming of those children? How did the mothers of that accursed offspring become sisters of their own children? How did the boys have the same man as both father and grandfather? Who confounded nature in lawlessness? Was it not wine exceeding its measure that brought on this incredible tragedy? Was it not drunkenness that wove into history a tale which in its extremes outdoes even true fables? "For they made their father drink wine," it says; and so, with his mind driven out by the wine, as if held by some sorcery, he left this tragic story to posterity, since drunkenness had stolen his senses from him at the moment of the abomination. O how wickedly those women carried wine with them out of the stores of Sodom! O what an evil loving-cup they poured out for their father from a wicked mixing-bowl! How much better it would have been for that wine too to perish in Sodom along with everything else, before it became the sponsor of such a tragedy! And though there are such examples, and so many evils from wine come into life every day, he [?] shamelessly pillories himself through his confession for having done this too: not only for having used wine, but for having taken care that the supply of such a possession should abound. "For I planted vineyards for myself," he says, vineyards I would have had no need of, had I myself become a thriving vine: a spiritual vine, luxuriant and spreading, intertwined with the branches of life and the tendrils of love toward its own kind, clothed not with leaves but with seemly conduct, and nurturing a ripe cluster of virtue.

He who plants these things in his own soul, cultivates the wine that gladdens the heart, and works his own land, as the proverb puts it and as the law of such husbandry requires, as it were hoeing [?] his life with his reasonings, pulling up the bastard growths that spring up beside the roots of the virtues, watering his soul with teachings, and with the pruning-hook of discerning reason cutting back the mind's drift toward what is superfluous and useless: such a man would be most blessed in his husbandry, pressing his own cluster into the mixing-bowl of wisdom. But the Preacher does not know this kind of planting, since he speaks with his face toward the earth and embraces its things. For to these he adds the ornaments of wealth, gardens and parks. What need of many parks has one who looks to the one Paradise? And what benefit is a garden to me, growing vegetables, the food of the weak? If I were in Paradise, I would not be dissipated in the desire for many parks. If I lived in health of soul, able to partake of more solid food, I would not busy myself with vegetables, gardening for myself the food suited to weakness. But once luxury has entered along with need, and desire has overstepped its limits, then after extravagance in houses and expense on vanities under a roof, a man goes on to pursue luxury in the open air too, and makes the very nature of the air serve his desire for pleasure. For trees are cultivated for him, evergreen and thick, serving as a roof against the sky, so that even out of doors he may live in luxury as if at home; and by the gardeners' art the face of the earth is clothed with every kind of plant, so that delights from every side meet the eye wherever he turns his gaze. He is always among the things he likes, and in every season of the year he sees what is out of season: grass in winter, early flowers, the vine trained up into the trees, interweaving its own branches with branches not its own, the elegant windings of ivy around the trees, and all those kinds of fruit which, crossed from different species, do violence to nature, showing in their look and taste that they belong to both, so that they seem to be both things at once, as happens when different kinds are blended. All these, and whatever else art has devised among plants by forcing nature, things that life's need never sought but undisciplined desire demands: all these, says the one who confesses his own deeds, came about through his elaborate craft in gardens and parks. For when he said, "I planted every fruit tree," this comprehensive phrase showed that nothing of the sort was left out. Then, after luxury out of doors and under a roof, not even water is left without its contribution to the supply of pleasures, as if he had to luxuriate in all the elements: in earth through its own products, in air through the trees, in water through a man-made sea. For so that the sight of water too might sweeten the deception of the eyes,

the ground becomes a lake, the water walled in all around, so that swimming may bring pleasure to those who bathe their bodies, and the overflow, divided off in every direction to meet the needs of what is watered, may make the parks more luxuriant. "For I made myself pools of water," he says, "to water from them a forest sprouting trees." Yet I had the spring of Paradise, that is, the teaching of the virtues, by which the drought of the soul was refreshed with dew, and I might have looked beyond earthly waters, whose enjoyment is short-lived and whose nature is fleeting. It would therefore be better for us to channel a small stream from the divine spring, through which the virtues of the soul spring up and are watered, so that the grove of good practices may flourish in our souls, through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power to the ages of ages. Amen.

The passage of confession still holds our discourse. For the one who recounts his own deeds goes through nearly everything that makes known the vanity of the affairs of this life. But now he touches, as it were, on a graver charge among his deeds, one that exposes the passion of pride. For what in the list is so much a matter of conceit (a costly house, a multitude of vines, the beauty of gardens and waters, the building of pools and the pastimes in the parks) as for one who is a human being to think himself master of his own kind? "I acquired," he says, "male and female slaves, and I had slaves born in my house." Do you see the swelling of arrogance? Such a statement rises up directly against God. For we have heard from the prophet that all things are the slaves of the power that is above all. So the one who makes God's possession his own possession, and claims dominion over his own kind, so as to think himself lord of men and women: what else is he doing but overstepping nature through pride, seeing himself as something different from those he rules? "I acquired male and female slaves." You condemn to slavery the human being, whose nature is free and self-determining, and you legislate against God, overturning his law for human nature. For the one who was made precisely to be lord of the earth, appointed to rule by his Maker, him you bring under the yoke of slavery, as if transgressing and fighting against the divine command. You have forgotten the limits of your authority: your rule is confined to having charge over the irrational creatures. For "let them rule," it says, "over birds and fish and four-footed beasts." How is it that you pass over the slavery that is subject to you and rise up against free nature itself, counting your own kind among the four-footed or even the footless creatures? "You have subjected all things to man," the Word cries through the prophet, and lists the things made subject to reason: "cattle, and oxen, and sheep."

Have human beings been born to you from cattle? Have oxen begotten human offspring for you? For the irrational creatures are the only slaves human beings have: "Making grass spring up for the cattle, and green plants for the service of men." But you have split nature into slavery and lordship, and made it slave to itself and lord over itself. "For I acquired male and female slaves." At what price, tell me? What did you find among all that exists that was worth as much as this nature? For how many coins did you value reason? For how many obols did you weigh out the image of God? For how many staters did you sell the nature that God fashioned? God said, "Let us make man in our image and likeness." He who is in the likeness of God, who rules all the earth, who received from God authority over all things on earth: tell me, who sells him, who buys him? This is in the power of God alone; or rather, hardly even of God himself. For "his gifts," it says, "are irrevocable." God, then, would not enslave our nature, since he called us back to freedom when we had enslaved ourselves to sin of our own will. But if God does not enslave the free, who sets his own power above God's? And how can the ruler of all the earth and of everything on earth be sold? For whatever belongs to the one sold must of necessity be sold along with him. At what price shall we value everything the whole earth holds? And if these things are beyond price, then what price, tell me, is he worth who is above them? Even if you say the whole world, not even so have you found a price equal to his worth. For he who knew human nature accurately said that not even the whole world was worth enough to be given in exchange for a man's soul. So when a human being is put up for sale, it is none other than the lord of the earth who is brought to the auction-block. Then clearly all the creation that belongs to him will be auctioned along with him: that is, earth and sea and islands, and everything in them. What then will the buyer put down? And what will the seller receive, when so great a property goes along with the transaction? But a little scrap of paper, a written contract and a count of obols have deceived you into thinking you are master of the image of God. What folly! If the contract were lost, if the writing were eaten away by moths, if a drop of water fell on it from somewhere and blotted it out, where would your pledges of slavery be? Where would your title to mastery be? For I see nothing more that the name gives you over your subject, apart from the name itself. What has this authority added to your nature? Not length of life, not any advantages. Your birth comes from the same source, your life is the same in kind; the passions of soul and body hold equal sway over you who are master and over him who is under the yoke of your mastery: pains and cheerfulness, joys and distresses, griefs and pleasures, angers and fears, sicknesses and deaths. Is there any difference in these things between master and slave? Do they not breathe in the same air? Do they not see the sun in the same way? Do they not alike, by taking in

food, sustain their nature? Are their inward parts not made the same way? Are the two not one dust after death? Is there not one judgment? Is the kingdom not shared, and Gehenna shared? You who are equal in everything, in what do you have more, tell me, that being a man you think yourself master of a man? "And I acquired," you say, "male and female slaves," as if they were a herd of goats or a drove of pigs. For having said, "I acquired male and female slaves," he added the satisfaction he had taken in his flocks and herds: "And I had great possessions of herds and flocks," he says, as though both these and those stood in the same rank, under the yoke of his power. Then, after these, the confession proceeds step by step to the greater sins; for he cries out against himself the root of all evils, which is the love of money. And he speaks, word for word, as follows: "I gathered for myself both silver and gold." What harm did gold do you while it lay mingled in the earth, spread through the places where the Creator set it from the beginning? What further debt did the Creator lay upon you, beyond the fruits of the earth? Did he not allot you only tree-fruits and seeds for food? Why do you overstep the bounds of your authority? Or else show me that these things too were granted you by the Creator: to mine and dig, to smelt the ore with fire, and to gather what you did not scatter. Or perhaps someone will reckon it no fault at all to gather money for oneself in this way from the mines of the earth? But since the text adds "the treasures of kings and of the provinces," the intention behind the gathering no longer tends toward innocence. For he says he collected gold and silver as if royal power were entitled to gather an abundance of money from the provinces, that is, to impose taxes, exact tithes, levy contributions and coerce its subjects. However it was done, I would gladly learn what more there will be for the one who gathers such material. Let us grant, for the sake of argument, that the lovers of money gain not by the mina or the drachma or the talent, but that everything is turned to gold for them at a stroke: the earth, the sand, the mountains, the plains, the glens. Let us suppose that everything has been changed all at once into this material: what would life gain from it toward happiness? If a man sees in everything what he now sees in a small amount, which of the goods of the soul, which of the things people strive for in the body, will such abundance bring about? Will there be any hope through this that one who lives amid so much gold will become wise, quick-witted, contemplative, learned, a friend of God, temperate, pure, free of passion, untouched by and closed to everything that drags one down toward vice? Or if not this, will it at least be possible for the body, stretching life out to many hundreds of years, ageless, free of sickness and harm, and everything [?] in life in the flesh? But

no one is so foolish, or so heedless of our common nature, as to think that these things would come to people even if the material of wealth were poured out for all in boundless abundance, as much as they pleased. For even now one can see many of those who excel in such wealth living in a pitiable body, who could not stay alive without their attendants if they were not at hand. If, then, the abundance of gold that our argument supposed for the sake of argument showed no gain for either body or soul, much more is the gold seen in small amounts proved useless for the benefit of its owners. For what could the material itself do for its owner, when it has no effect on taste, or smell, or hearing, and to the touch is no different from any other hard object? And let no one credit gold with the food or clothing obtained by exchange. For he who exchanged gold for bread or a cloak traded the useless for the useful, and he lives by making bread his food, not gold. But he who gathered this material for himself through such exchanges, what profit did he have from his money? What counsel did it give, what instruction in affairs, what foreknowledge of the future? Who ever found relief from bodily pain in it? He counted it, stored it, sealed it with his seal; when asked for it, he denied having it; when disbelieved, he even swore an oath. This is his blessedness, this the goal of his zeal, this his enjoyment, this the extent of his happiness: to secure the material by perjury. "But gold," he says, "has a beautiful colour." Is it more beautifully coloured than fire? Lovelier than the stars? Brighter than the rays of the sun? Who keeps you from enjoying these, so that you have to procure pleasure for your eyes from the colour of gold? "But fire goes out," he says, "and the sun sets, and the charm of their brightness does not last." And what difference, tell me, is there between gold and lead in the dark? "But," he says, "we could not get necklaces and bracelets, brooches and belts, collars and crowns and such things from fire or from the stars; but gold makes these, and anything else devised for adornment." This defence of the material has carried zeal to the very height of vanity. For I would put this very question to them: what is a man after when he decks his hair with gold, or hangs ornaments from his ears, or wraps his neck in luxurious necklaces, or wears gold displayed on some other part of the body? Wherever on the body it happens to be put on show, he himself is in no way transformed into the gleam of the gold. For whoever looks at the gold-wearer sees the gold just as it would look lying in the shops, but sees the wearer just as he is by nature. Even if the gold is finely wrought and engraved, even if it holds green or fiery gems set in it, nature has gained no more sensation from what lies beside it; but if there is some disfigurement of the face, or something lacking that nature should supply, or a discharge from the eye [?]

[?] If, then, it contributes nothing useful to those who strive after it, neither for beauty, nor for bodily health, nor for the relief of pain, why is it so eagerly sought? And what is the state of mind of those whose hearts are melted into this material, when, aware of possessing such things, they exult in themselves as if they had something more than others? If someone were to ask them whether they would accept having their nature changed into that thing, and becoming what they have honoured with such affection, would they choose the change, so that their nature passed from human to gold, and they were shown to be no longer rational and thinking and using their senses for life, but pale and heavy and speechless, soulless and senseless, as the nature of gold is? I do not think they would choose this, not even those who are utterly melted into the material by their desire. If, then, sensible people already count it a curse to take on the properties of soulless matter, what irrational madness is it to pursue the possession of things whose end is vanity, so that those driven mad by money even dare murder and robbery for it? And not only this, but also the wicked device of interest, or "offspring" as it is called, which one would not be wrong to call another form of robbery and bloodshed. For what difference is there between secretly breaking through a wall and holding another's goods as plunder, or murdering a traveller and making oneself master of his belongings, and acquiring what does not belong to one through the compulsion of interest?
