O evil name! Robbery is called "offspring." O bitter marriages! O wicked union, which nature never knew, but which the disease of the money-lovers has invented among lifeless things! O grievous pregnancies, from which such offspring is born! Among all that exists, only living things were divided by the difference of male and female. To them God who formed them said, "Increase and multiply," so that by being born from one another living things might grow into a multitude. But the "offspring" of gold, from what marriage does it come? From what pregnancy is it brought to term? Yet I know the birth-pangs of such offspring, having learned them from the prophet: "Behold, he travailed with injustice, conceived trouble, and brought forth lawlessness." This is that offspring with which greed travails, which lawlessness brings forth, and which hatred of mankind delivers as midwife. For the man who always hides his wealth and swears on oath that he has nothing, when he sees someone choked by necessity, then shows himself pregnant in his purse; then, out of love of gain, he goes into labour with his wicked offspring and holds out to the unfortunate man the [?] of a loan, which he heaps on the misfortune like fuel, like someone trying to put out a flame with oil. For he did not heal the loss with his loan, but made it worse; and just as fields in a drought bear thorns of their own accord, so too in [?]

…on the misfortunes of those in distress, the interest charged by the greedy grows wild. Then he holds out his hand with the money, as a fishing line holds out the hook hidden in the bait. The poor wretch gapes at the plenty in front of him, and with the tug of the hook he vomits up whatever he had hidden away in storage. Such are the benefits of interest! If someone takes another's provisions by force, or steals them in secret, he is called violent, a robber, and the like. But the one who has his injustice witnessed and his cruelty put on record, and confirms his lawlessness with contracts, is called humane and a benefactor and a saviour, and is given every good name there is. Gain made by pilfering is called theft. Yet the one who strips Christ naked through this kind of compulsion gives his cruelty the pet name of kindness, for that is what they call the losses of the wretched. "I gathered for myself both silver and gold." The wise man, instructing human life, counted this too in the list of what he confessed. He did so for a reason. People can learn from one who has condemned it by experience that this is among the things condemned as wrong, and so guard against the assault of evil before they experience it themselves. In the same way one can pass unharmed through country full of bandits and wild beasts, because others have gone ahead and braved the danger there. The divine Apostle defines the passion of avarice well, very well, when he declares it the root of all evils. When a corrupt and putrid humour flows into some part of the body and the place becomes inflamed, the lodged fluid must break out into an abscess and decay, as the infected matter escapes to the surface. In the same way, in those into whom the disease of love of money flows, the passion mostly breaks out into licentiousness. This is why, after the abundance of gold and silver, he adds the indecency that naturally follows the disease that had already taken hold. "For I made," he says, "male and female singers" (the luxuries of banquets), "cupbearers male and female." Merely mentioning the names was enough to expose the passion for which the disease of money had paved the way. O this perverse ingenuity! How it pours in the flood of pleasures all at once, deluging souls with twin torrents through hearing and sight, so that evil may be both seen and heard! Song overthrows the hearing; the spectacle overpowers the [?]. On one side, the female voice, through the loose harmony of the songs, carries passion with it into the heart. On the other, sight falls like a siege engine on the eyes of a man already undone by the songs, and overthrows the soul. The general of this battle line is wine. Like a wicked archer, it shoots at the man with two kinds of arrows and aims its points at both hearing and sight: the song becomes the arrow for the hearing, and the spectacle the arrow for the sight. "Cupbearers" is not a mere name; the title certainly comes from the task. When

therefore unmixed wine is poured out lavishly for the drinkers, and young people trained to beauty wait on them in this service, whether boys made effeminate by their finery, or the female sex itself moving about the banquet and confusing the mind with toasts until it thinks unseemly thoughts, where are such pursuits likely to end? As for the man who makes each of these things his aim and goes beyond need into elaboration, how he will dress the women who make music in song, what kind of robe he will put on the women who pour the wine: such things are better passed over in silence. The discourse should not linger over describing them, lest even in denouncing them the memory should scratch open the wounds of those more given to passion. For these things the gold, for these the silver, so that it may provide such baits of luxury. Perhaps this is why Scripture calls the passion of pleasure a serpent. It is a serpent's nature that if its head slips into a joint in a wall, it draws the whole length of its body in after it. I mean something like this. Nature makes a dwelling necessary for human beings. But through this need pleasure slips into the joints of the soul, diverts the need into a boundless extravagance of ornament, and changes the whole aim of the effort. Then the beast, pleasure, creeps on to vineyards and pools and parks and the decorations of gardens. After this it rears its head in arrogance and coils itself in conceit, having yoked rule over its fellow human beings to itself. On top of this it drags along the coil of love of money, which licentiousness necessarily follows: the last part, the tail, of the beast that pleasure makes of us. But a snake cannot be pulled back out by its tail, because its scales naturally resist anyone pulling in the opposite direction. In the same way one cannot start from the last parts in evicting the creeping thing of pleasure from the soul, unless one shuts off evil's first entrance. That is why the teacher of virtue tells us to watch its head. He calls the beginning of evil the head; if that is not let in, the rest can do nothing. Whoever has set himself against pleasure as a whole will not be carried away by the passion's partial assaults; but whoever has admitted the beginning of the passion has taken the whole beast in with it. For this reason, having gone through everything, the one who makes such passions public sums up his discourse under a heading. At the beginning he said, "I made my work great"; now he concludes the detailed account of what happened with "I became great." He is showing that his knowledge of the opposite things did not come to him through small matters. His experience reached the very utmost greatness, so that nothing remembered of anyone before him could equal it. For he says, "I became great," and added, "beyond

all who were before me in Jerusalem." And now he has revealed the purpose for which, already trained in all wisdom, he went down to experience such things: "My wisdom," he says, "stood by me." By these words he means: through wisdom I searched out every means of enjoyment ever devised, and my mind stands at the summit of everything found in these things. My sight worked together with my desire, and through the pleasure of the eyes my will was filled with whatever it craved, so that nothing devised for enjoyment was left out. Instead, sharing in pleasures became my portion and possession. To me this seems to mean nothing other than: I took into myself every means of enjoyment ever devised, reaping gladness from what was done as one reaps it from a possession. "For I did not hold back my heart from any gladness, and my heart rejoiced in all my toil, and this became my portion from all my toil." By "portion" he means possession. He has gone through the luxury in detail, running from beginning to end. He has recounted in his discourse everything that stirs up pleasures in those who enjoy them: the beauty of buildings, the vineyards, the gardens, the pools, the parks, rule over his fellow human beings, abundance of wealth, the preparations for delight at banquets, all the "luxuries," as he calls them. His wisdom was occupied with these, searching them out and devising them, and he says he enjoyed them through every sense, his eyes finding whatever gave pleasure and his soul having every desire unhindered. Then he explains the first utterance he made at the opening of the discourse, when he declared that all things are vanity. Looking at these things, he says, he declares concerning human life that whatever the senses see and whatever people pursue for gladness is all vanity. "For I looked on all my works that my hands had done, and on all the toil with which I toiled to do them, and behold, all was vanity and a choice of the wind, and there is no profit under the sun." All the power and activity of the senses is bounded by life under the sun. The sensing nature cannot cross beyond it and come to understand the goods that lie above. Having examined all these things and others like them, then, he teaches human life not to admire anything here: wealth, ambition, rule over subjects, delights and luxuries and banquets, or anything else considered precious. He teaches us instead to see that the one end of all such things is vanity, and that no profit from it is found afterwards. Those who write on water do perform the writing with their hand, tracing the shapes of the letters in the liquid, yet

nothing of the marks keeps its shape. The effort of writing exists only in the act of writing, because the surface of the water always follows the hand and smooths out what was inscribed. In the same way every effort and activity of enjoyment appears only while it is going on. When the activity stops, the enjoyment too is wiped out. Nothing is stored up for afterwards. No trace of gladness is left to those who took pleasure, no remnant of the activity of pleasure once it has passed. This is what the text means when it says there is no profit under the sun for those who labour at such things, whose end is vanity. May we too be free of them, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power to the ages of ages. Amen.

Now the great leader of the Church initiates us into the loftier teachings. In the preceding discourses he first cleansed our souls and drew them away from every desire for vanity that arises in human beings. Only then does he bring the mind to the truth, once it has shaken off the burden of vain things like a load from its shoulders. Let the Church be taught this as a doctrine, learning from the present teaching that the beginning of the virtuous life is to get clear of evil. The great David too, in the psalms, gives a kind of introductory guide to the pure way of life, and he does not begin from the perfection contemplated in the beatitude. He did not say first that blessed is the one who prospers in all things, who is like the tree rooted by the streams of water, who stays ever green in good things, who gathers the fruits of life in their proper seasons. Instead he made turning away from evil the beginning of blessedness, since it is impossible to become good before washing off the filth of evil. So too this great Ecclesiastes first removes vain things by his discourse, so that, as in a sick body, the good of health may then come about. That is why he ran through his discourse on vanity. He said that the senses are not a safe criterion of the good, he brought into view the unreality in what people pursue, and he separated our faculty of desire from bodily enjoyment. In this way he points out what is truly to be chosen and truly desirable. Pursuing it is something active and substantial. It remains forever with those who seek it and is separate from every notion of vanity. Chapter 2, verse 12: "For I looked," he says, "to see wisdom." That is: in order to see clearly what I longed for, I first looked at distraction and folly too. Setting a thing beside its opposite makes our view of what we pursue clearer. He also calls wisdom counsel, when he says, "What man is there who will come after

the counsel, in all that it has done?" He teaches, then, what human wisdom is: to follow the true wisdom. He also calls this true wisdom counsel, the maker of things that truly are and subsist and are not seen in vanity. This is the sum of human wisdom. True wisdom and counsel, in my view at least, is nothing other than the wisdom conceived before the universe. This is the wisdom in which God made all things, as the Prophet says: "In wisdom you have made all things." Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, in whom all things came into being and were set in order. Human wisdom, then, is to come to understand the true works of the true wisdom and counsel. And the work of that counsel, or wisdom, is in my view incorruptibility, the blessedness of the soul, courage, justice, prudence, and every name and idea understood in terms of virtue. If so, perhaps it follows that we are brought to the knowledge of what is good. "For I saw these things," he says, "and weighed what is against what is not, as on a scale, to find the difference between wisdom and folly," as great a difference as one would find in comparing light with darkness. And it seems fitting to me that he used the example of light for the good. Darkness by its own nature has no real existence: if nothing blocked the sun's ray, there would be no darkness. Light, however, exists in and of itself and is understood in its own substance. So by this example he shows that evil does not subsist of itself but exists only alongside, as a privation of the good. The good, on the other hand, is always the same, abiding and firm, and does not exist alongside any prior privation. What is thought of as the opposite of the good has no substantial existence, for what does not exist in itself is nothing at all. Evil is a privation of being, not an existence. The difference between wisdom and folly, then, is equal to that between light and darkness. Using a part for the whole, he includes all good under the name of wisdom, and by folly he signifies the whole nature of evil. But what do we gain from admiring the good unless the teacher also shows us some road to acquiring it? How then can we too come to share in the good? Let us hear the teacher. "The wise man's eyes," he says, "are in his head." What are you saying? Is there any creature at all that has its organs of sight outside its head, whether you mean those living in water, on land or in the air? In all of them the eye is set at the front of the rest of the body and lodged in the head, in those that have a head. How then can he say here that only the wise man's head has eyes? Surely he is hinting by this that there is a certain correspondence between what is observed in the soul and the parts of the body. Just as in the structure of the body the part that leads the whole is called the head,

so too in the soul the ruling and leading part is understood as its head. And just as we call the base of the foot the heel, so the soul too would have a base. By this it touches its union with the body, and from there it imparts the power and activity of sensation to the body beneath it. When the soul's power of discernment and contemplation is occupied with things of sense, the nature of its eyes shifts down to its heels. Through them it sees what is below and is left unable to see lofty sights. But if it recognizes the vanity of what lies below and lifts its gaze to its own head, which is Christ, as Paul explains, it would be blessed for its keen sight, since it has its eyes where evil casts no darkness. The great Paul had his eyes in the head, as did any others great like him, and as do all who live and move and have their being in Christ. One who is in the light cannot see darkness; in the same way, one who has his eye in Christ cannot fix his gaze on anything vain. We have understood the head to be the beginning of all things. So whoever has his eyes in the head has his eyes in all virtue (for Christ is complete virtue): in truth, in justice, in incorruptibility, in every good. "The wise man's eyes, then, are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness." For whoever does not set his lamp on the lampstand but puts it under the bed has made the light darkness for himself and become the maker of something unreal. And the vain is the unreal, so darkness means the same thing as the vain. The fool's soul, then, having become body-loving and fleshly, sees nothing when it looks at these things; keen sight in such matters is in truth darkness. Look at those sharp and versatile people in everyday life whom we call lawyers. See how they make injustice easy for themselves with witnesses, advocates, documents and the courting of judges, so as both to commit wrong and to escape punishment. Who does not admire the shrewdness and versatility of such people? Yet they are blind when measured against that eye which sees what is above and is set in the head of all that exists. They are plainly blind, these people who adorn their own heel, the heel that is torn by the serpent's teeth. Through the eyes with which they look downward they engrave the doctrines of sin on themselves. "For whoever loves injustice hates his own soul," and what people count blessed in them is more pitiable than any misfortune. On the other hand, how many people, filled with the struggles on high and occupied with contemplating the things that truly are, are thought blind and useless in material affairs! Paul too boasts of being such a man when he says he is a fool for Christ's sake. His prudence and wisdom were not occupied with anything that is pursued here. That is why he says, "We are fools for Christ's

sake," as if he were saying: we are blind to the life below because we look above and have our eyes in the head. For this reason he was homeless and had no table of his own; he was poor, a wanderer, naked, worn down by hunger and thirst. But consider what this man, so poor here below, was like in the things above. He was caught up as far as the third heaven, where his head was, and there he had his eyes. He rejoiced in the ineffable mysteries of paradise, saw what cannot be seen, and delighted in things beyond sense and thought. Who would not have thought him pitiable, seeing him a prisoner, tortured with blows, and in shipwreck plunged into the deep and carried over the sea by the waves, chains and all? Yet although his circumstances among human beings were like this, he never turned away from keeping his eyes always in the head, saying: "Who will separate us from the love of Christ that is in Christ Jesus? Affliction, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword?" This is the same as saying: Who will gouge my eyes out of the head and move them to what is earthly and trodden underfoot? And he bids us do the same when he commands us to set our minds on things above, which amounts to saying we should have our eyes in the head. Now that we have learned how the wise man's eyes are in his head, let us flee folly, which becomes darkness for those who walk through this life. "For the fool," he says, "walks in darkness." And the fool, as the prophecy says, is the one who says in his heart that there is no God, who has become corrupt and abominable in his ways. In what follows, the course of the text treats those who are small-souled about this life. They think death something grievous, and so they believe that those who pursue the higher life gain nothing from living virtuously. Life, they say, ends at the same point for both, and there is no escaping death, unless one should succeed through a more [?] life. He raises these objections as if in his own person, then turns on the absurdity of those who put them forward, since they have given no thought to the nature of reality. He teaches the difference, and where virtue has the advantage over vice: no equality of honour is to be expected between them just because they share in death; the difference lies in the good or evil things that await us hereafter. The words of the objection run as follows: "I knew that one fate will befall them all. And I said in my heart: As the fate of the fool, so it will befall me too. Why then have I become exceedingly wise? I spoke in my heart, since the fool speaks out of excess, that this too is vanity. For there is no remembrance of the wise man together with the fool forever, since already the days

…coming, all things have been forgotten; and how shall the wise man die together with the fool?” To this he adds that he came to think everything worthy of hatred that he had once been passionately attached to, when he embraced what is vain as though it were good. He says that he hated everything he had laboured at with an eye to this life, because he laboured at all of it not for himself but for the one who would come after him. Since the future is uncertain, he cannot know in advance how that person will use what was laboured for. These are his exact words: “And I hated life, because the work that is done under the sun is evil to me, for all is vanity and a choice of the spirit. And I hated all my toil, which I toil at under the sun, because I leave it to the man who comes after me. And who knows whether he will be wise or foolish, and whether he will have power over all my toil in which I toiled and in which I grew wise under the sun? This too is vanity.” After saying this, he says that his soul also turned against the idea that the person who has lived virtuously and the person who has made no effort toward virtue have one and the same portion. For the one, he says, toils in wisdom, knowledge and courage. The other toils in anger and in the pains that come with anxious effort over a livelihood. To put these two on an equal footing is, he says, not only vanity but also wickedness. This passage runs as follows: “And I turned to renounce in my heart all my toil which I toiled at under the sun, because there is a man whose toil is in wisdom and in knowledge and in courage, and to a man who did not toil in it he will give his portion. This too is vanity and wickedness. For what comes to a man in all his toil and in the choice of his heart, in which he toils under the sun? For all his days are days of pain, and his distraction is one of anger, and even at night his heart does not rest. This too is vanity.” Next he puts to himself another objection, raised by those who judge the life of pleasure preferable to the higher life. He refutes it, setting out both the objection and its answer in his own person. The objection is that nothing should be thought good except what a person takes into himself, and that means eating and drinking. The answer is that what nourishes and gladdens a human being is not these things but wisdom and knowledge. It is good, then, to devote one’s effort to these. What is pursued through the flesh is distraction of soul and vanity. The words of this lofty teaching run like this: “There is nothing good for a man but what he will eat and drink, and so show his soul good in his toil. And this too I saw, that it is from the hand of God; for who will eat and drink apart from him? For to the man who is good before his face he has given wisdom and knowledge and gladness, and to the sinner he has given distraction, to add and to gather,

to give to the one who is good before the face of God. For this too is vanity and a choice of the spirit.” This, then, is the sense of what is written next, and this is the preliminary view of the sequence, which we have now briefly set out. It is time to take up the text again and fit the thoughts precisely to the words. “And I too knew that one event will befall them all. And I said, ‘As the event of the fool, so it will befall me too; why then did I become wise?’” This is the objection he raises against himself. He is saying: if the event of death is one and the same for both, and virtue does not exempt the person who has become wise from sharing in death, then my zeal for wisdom has been in vain. The reply of the text to these words is this: “I,” he says, “spoke this superfluously in my heart, because a fool speaks out of superfluity. And this too is vanity. For there is no memory of the wise man with the fool for ever.” He condemns this objection as brought in superfluously and illogically [?]. He calls this reasoning foolish because it is not one of the things laid up in store, nor is it brought out from within, from the treasuries of wisdom. It is a kind of superfluous discharge of the mind, spat out like foam. For “a fool speaks out of superfluity.” To use reasoning in this way is vain and leads to nothing, since its only aim is to persuade us not to look beyond what appears. The objector wages his battle with visible things, and death is one of the things that appear. What, then, does he mean? He means that the judgment between the virtuous life and the wicked life is not made in this, as though only the wicked had to die in the body while the good remained untouched by bodily death. The objector does not know in what the immortality of virtue lies, or what death is for those who live in vice. The memory of the wise man, he says, lives for ever and stretches on through all the ages, but for the fool even the memorial has been quenched. For of such people the Prophet also says, “Their memorial has perished with a sound,” that is, conspicuously and plainly; this is what the addition “with a sound” shows. So, he says, there is no memory of the wise man with the fool for ever. The life of the wise man lasts for ever through memory, while oblivion takes the place of the fool. In the days to come, everything belonging to the fool passes into oblivion. This is what he always means by the words “since already, as the days come, all things have been forgotten.” If, then, the wise man seeks wisdom while the fool has vanished in the death of oblivion, how, he says, can you say that the wise man will die together with the fool? That is why he is pained and ashamed at what he pursued in this life, and says that he hates all he strove for with this life in view. He is like a man who greedily and shamelessly gorged himself on poisoned honey. Once his indulgence has turned into a bad humour inside him, he vomits, and only then does he taste the poison mixed in, which comes up together with the honey. And for this reason,

remembering his disgust, he hates honey, because through the poison his surfeit brought on his sickness. In the same way the Preacher had filled himself to satiety with everything sought for luxury. Now, in the vomiting of confession, he loathes and abhors the shame of his deeds as if it were the taste of some poison, and he cries out that he hates that life. These are his exact words: “And I hated life, because the work that is done under the sun is evil to me.” For I became evil, he says, to no one else but myself through what I did under the sun. None of what was done stood firm for me. Everything I strove for was mere conceit and an impulse of the will. “For all is vanity and a choice of the spirit,” he says. He also says that effort spent here deserves hatred, because one toils not for oneself but for whoever comes after. Whatever a person may have achieved by effort in this life — dockyards, harbours, splendid and costly fortifications and buildings, gateways and towers, beautiful colonnades and monuments, the labours of the land, groves of every kind, lovely meadows, vineyards as broad as the sea, and anything else of the sort — the one who happened to labour at it toiled, but the one who enters life after him gets the share. And it is uncertain whether he will not turn that wealth into material for vice. It is not for everyone to let their senses down into the experience of such things for the sake of knowledge. Yet I, he says, did this through wisdom. With full control, I let the impulse of nature frisk a little, like a colt, among the lower passions, and then I bridled it again with the rein of reason and brought it back under reason’s authority. Who knows, he says, whether the one who comes after us into these things, whoever he may be, will be master of their enjoyment, and not rather be mastered by them, bowing like a slave to the tyranny of pleasure? That is why, he says, “I hated all my toil which I toil at under the sun, because I leave it to the man who comes after me. And who knows whether he will be wise or foolish, and whether he will have power over all my toil in which I toiled and in which I grew wise under the sun?” This, I think, is the meaning of this saying: that he himself did not by passion toward the

…toils, and does not draw his desire down to anything merely human. The other, on the contrary, endures none of the toils that belong to virtue and wears himself out only in bodily labours. So when someone casts the vote for the good in favour of this second man and overlooks the one who excels in wisdom, he declares this unjust judgment to be not only vain but wicked. He puts it in these words: “And I turned,” he says, “to make my heart renounce the other toil which I toiled at under the sun.” What, then, did I renounce? That there is a man whose toil is in wisdom and knowledge and courage, and another man who has toiled at nothing of the kind. How, then, could anyone award the portion of preference to such a man? For “to a man who toiled in it,” he says, that is, to the one who has toiled at his life in the good [?], “he will give his portion.” This stands for: “he will reckon such a life as having the lot of the good.” But this, he says, is vanity and great wickedness. How is it not great wickedness, when he knows the effort and the will that are set in a person toward his toils? This is what he means when he says: “For he knows, concerning man, in all his toil and in the choice of his heart, in which he toils under the sun.” What, then, is it that he knows? “That all his days,” he says, “are days of pain, and his distraction is one of anger. And even at night his heart does not rest.” For truly, those who busy their souls with this temptation have a painful life, which lashes the heart with desires for more as if with goads. Their striving after gain is full of pain. It is not so much gladdened by what it has as pained by what it lacks. Their toil is divided between night and day and works through each in turn: the day is spent in labours, and the night drives sleep from their eyes, for anxieties about profit knock sleep away. How, then, can anyone who looks at these things fail to condemn the vanity of such effort? That is why he adds to what he said before: “This too is vanity.” Then he takes up another objection, which runs like this: “If you count what is outside us among vain things, O teacher, then what we take into ourselves cannot reasonably be condemned as vain. But eating and drinking take place within us. So such a thing is not to be rejected; rather, one should regard such a grace as a divine benefit.” That is the sense of the objection, and the words run like this: “There is nothing good,” he says, “in a man, but what he will eat and drink, and so show his soul good in his toil. And this too I saw, that it is from the hand of God, that anyone will drink apart from him [?].” This is the objection that the advocate of gluttony puts to the teacher. But in reply the guide to wisdom speaks of “the man who is good,” and the addition of the word “good” clearly also shows the distinction,

so that what is meant by its opposite, goodness, is made plain. It was not for a grazing beast [?], nor for the man bent over his own belly, who has a gullet in place of reason, but for the good man, who lives in the image of the only Good, that God did not ordain [?] this luxury at which the brutish nature gapes. Instead, he says, he gave him wisdom and knowledge and gladness. How could anyone grow in goodness through foods for the belly? “Man shall not live by bread alone.” This is the word of the true Word. Virtue is not nourished by bread. The strength of the soul does not thrive and grow fat on meat. The lofty life is nourished and made strong by other foods. The food of the good is temperance. Its bread is wisdom, its relish is justice, and its drink is freedom from passion. Its pleasure is not the body’s pleasure, such as the attachment to what suits one’s appetite, but the pleasure whose name and nature is gladness. That is why he gave this name to the soul’s disposition toward the good: such a state comes from being right-minded. So here too we should learn what we have also heard from the Apostle, that the kingdom of God is not eating and drinking but righteousness, freedom from passion and blessedness. What people strive for for the sake of bodily enjoyment is the pursuit of sinners and a distraction of the soul, which is dragged down from things above to things below. The whole span of such a soul’s life in this world is spent in the effort to add and to gather. Anyone, then, who judges this to be good before the face of God does not realise that he is locating the good in what is vain. These things I have said in my own voice, but setting the divine words beside them will seal this meaning. For he says: “To the sinner he gave distraction, to add and to gather, to give to the one who is good before the face of God. For this too is vanity and a choice of the spirit.” Whatever, then, we have learned in the present reading from this side-by-side examination of the good and the worse, may it be a help to us in [?] avoiding what has been condemned, and provision for [?] the better things rightly achieved.

HOMILY VI. “For all things there is a time, and a season for every matter under heaven.” This is the beginning of the sayings set before us for study. The labour of examining them is not small, and the gain from that labour [?] is worth [?] the labour. For perhaps the aim of what we have studied in the [?] parts of the book is made most clear in this section, as the discourse will show as it goes on step by step. In the previous discourses, everything people strive for that brings no gain to the soul was condemned as vain. The good was pointed out, to which we must look through the thoughts that lie in the head, and the delight that comes with wisdom was set against those who put forward bodily enjoyment. What remains is to learn how one might live according to virtue, receiving, as it were, a kind of art and method

for setting life right through reason. This, then, is what the present examination of the words promises us at the outset, where it declares: “For all things there is a time, and a season for every matter under heaven.” If one looks into the depth of the meaning, one will find a great deal of philosophy contained in these words, both contemplative and advising what is beneficial. To give ourselves a brief way into the study of this saying, we shall divide the argument as follows. Of the things that exist, some are material and perceptible by the senses, while others are intelligible and immaterial. Of these, the incorporeal lies beyond the grasp of the senses, and we shall know it only when we have stripped off the senses. Sense, which grasps the material nature, cannot pass beyond the heavenly body or penetrate to what lies beyond appearances. That is why the text speaks to us about earthly and heavenly things, so that we may live among them without stumbling. This life is material, a life lived through the flesh, and the contemplation of the good is somehow darkened by what appears to the senses. So we need a kind of science for judging the good, so that, as with a rule or a plumb-line in building, everything we do may be kept straight. This is what the text shows us in advance, and through it life is directed toward what it ought to be. For he says that in life there are two criteria of the good for each thing we strive for in this life: due measure and right timing. This is what he now teaches when he says: “For all things there is a time, and a season for every matter.” By “time” we should understand measure, because time stretches alongside everything that comes to be. Whether these criteria of the good are suitable for every achievement of virtue without exception, I do not yet affirm, until the discourse shows it as it goes on. But that the greater part of an ordered life is achieved by observing them, anyone can see. Who does not know that virtue, too, is a measure, measured by the mean between the things considered alongside it? Nothing that falls short of the proper measure, or overshoots it, could be virtue. Take courage: its deficiency becomes cowardice, and its excess becomes rashness. That is why some of the wise men from outside, who were perhaps thieves of what is ours, divided between them the meaning expressed in this saying. One gave the advice in a maxim that nothing should be lacking, and the other forbade excess: one declared that “measure is best,” and the other laid down “nothing too much.” Both show that falling short of the measure that virtue seeks is to be condemned, and overshooting due proportion is to be rejected. The same account will be given us about right timing: neither what comes before the right time nor what lags behind it is judged to be good. What good would it do the farmer to undertake [?] the cutting of the ears before

the crops have ripened in their season, or to put off the work of harvesting until the seeds have dropped from the stalk? In neither case does his effort achieve anything good. Whichever way he misses the season, he loses its benefit by cutting at the wrong time. And what has been said about one case can be seen in all. Seafaring, too, knows the same [?] harm, whether one goes before the right moment or lags behind it. And need one speak of medicine, and how much harm comes from overshooting or falling short of the proper time and measure of treatment? But we must leave these things aside, since the example will be made clearer in what follows, in the very words of the Ecclesiast. Why, then, have we considered these things beforehand? Because neither what lacks measure nor what is untimely is good. What is fine and worth choosing is what has its perfection through both. If someone attends to only one of them and the other is neglected, even what was done rightly will be useless because of what is lacking. We move by working both our feet. If something happens to one of them, the sound one is also useless for running because its partner is weak. In the same way, if timing lacks measure, or measure lacks timing, what is present is made entirely useless along with what is lacking. Proportion is useful when it is in season, and timeliness is useful when it is in measure. So we have understood “time” as standing for measure, because time is the measure of every particular measure. Whatever comes to be certainly comes to be in time, and the span of time stretches alongside the extent of each thing that comes to be: a little time for what is lesser, more time for what is greater. There is a measure of pregnancy, a measure of the growth of the ears of grain, a measure of the ripening of fruits, a measure of a voyage, a measure of a journey, and a measure of each stage of life: infant, small child, lad, boy, adolescent, man, middle-aged, mature, past one’s prime, elderly, old man. The measure that time provides is not one and the same for all things. Because the subjects differ, it is impossible for all things to be of equal measure with one another. But, as has been said, time is the common measure of everything measured, and it contains all things in itself. That is why he did not say “a measure for all things,” because things measured are very unequal [?] in being more and less. Instead he said “a time for all things,” meaning the general measure against which everything that comes to be is measured. Consider human life. What is advanced in years is weak, and what is not yet settled is disorderly. Best is the mean between the two, which escapes the drawbacks of both. In it we see the strength of youth freed from its disorder, and the prudence of old age freed from its feebleness, so that there is strength blended with prudence, avoiding equally the feebleness of old age and the rashness of youth. In the same way, he who sets a time for all things uses his words to separate off, on either side, the vice that comes from lack of measure, both the

…disregarding what goes beyond the proper time and rejecting what falls short of it. But now it may be time for the study of the inspired words themselves to be set before us in order. "A time," he says, "to give birth, and a time to die." He did well to yoke this inevitable pair together at the very start of his discourse, joining death to birth. For death necessarily follows birth, and everything that comes into being dissolves into decay. By showing death and birth joined together, he means to use the remembrance of death as a kind of goad, to rouse those who are sunk deep in the life of the flesh and stir them to care for what is to come. Moses, the friend of God, teaches the same wisdom covertly in the very first titles of his books, placing Exodus immediately after Genesis, so that those who read the titles might be taught about their own condition by the very order of the books. For no one can hear of a genesis without at once thinking of an exodus. The great Ecclesiastes understood this and shows it here too, presenting death as the counterpart of birth. For "a time to give birth," he says, "and a time to die." The time came, he says, and I was born; the time will come, and I shall die. If we all kept our eyes on this, we would not leave the short road and go round in circles with the ungodly, wandering of our own accord along life's roundabout path of error, among powers and honors and riches. Entangled by these in the many roads of this life, we can no longer find the way out of the labyrinth of this life, and by the very things we seem to pursue so eagerly we confuse for ourselves the signs of the road that does not stray. How blessed indeed, he says, are those among men who leave behind life's circuitous deceptions and set themselves on the short road of virtue! And this road consists in turning the soul toward none of the things here, but in straining with zeal toward what is set before us, through faith, in hope. But let us examine the saying again. "A time," he says, "to give birth, and a time to die." Would that my birth too might come in its proper time, and my death be timely! For no one would say that Ecclesiastes is here holding up this involuntary [?] and death that comes of itself as an achievement of virtue. Labor pains do not depend on the woman's will, nor does death lie in the choice of those who die. And what is not in our power no one would classify as either virtue or vice. So we must work out what a timely birth is, and what a death that comes at the right time is. To my mind a birth is mature and not abortive when, as Isaiah says, someone conceives from the fear of God and, through the labor pains of the soul, gives birth to his own salvation. For in a sense we become our own fathers when, through good choice, we form ourselves, give birth to ourselves, and bring ourselves into

the light. We do this by receiving God into ourselves, becoming children of God, children of power, and sons of the Most High. And again we miscarry ourselves and make ourselves fruitless, like wind-eggs, when, as the Apostle says, "the form of Christ" is not formed in us. For the man of God, he says, must be complete. And that man is entirely complete in whom the principle of nature has been perfectly fulfilled. So if someone has made himself a child of God through virtue, receiving the power for this noble birth, he has known the time of good labor, and he rightly rejoices, as the Gospel says, that a human being has been born into the world. But one who has become a child of wrath, a son of perdition, an offspring of darkness, a brood of vipers, an evil offspring, and all the other names by which a wicked birth is denounced, has not known the life-giving time. For there is one time that gives birth to life, not many. Whoever misses it through an untimely birth has brought himself forth into perdition and delivered his soul to death. And if it is clear how we are born in due time, it is plain to all how we die in due time, as for holy Paul every moment was a fitting time for a good death. For he cries out in his own words, making a kind of oath: "I die every day, I swear by my boasting in you"; and, "For your sake we are being put to death all day long"; and, "We ourselves had the sentence of death within ourselves." And it is surely not hard to see how Paul dies every day. He never lives to sin; he always puts to death the members of the flesh and carries about in himself the dying of the body of Christ; he is always crucified with Christ; he never lives to himself but has Christ living in him. In our judgment at least, this would be the timely death, the one that brings about true life. "For I," he says, "will kill, and I will make alive," so that we may be truly convinced that it is God's gift to be put to death to sin and made alive by the Spirit. For through killing, the divine voice promises to give life. What follows is similar to what has been said: "A time," he says, "to plant, and a time to pluck up what has been planted." We know who our farmer is, and whose field we are. The first we have learned from Christ, the second from Paul, Christ's servant. For the Lord says, "My Father is the farmer," and the Apostle says to us, "You are God's field." So the great farmer knows how to plant only what is good. "For God planted a garden in Eden, toward the east." And what is contrary to the good he plucks up. "For every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up." Therefore the wickedness and unbelief of the Pharisees, and their ingratitude for the miracles performed by the

Lord: these are the plants that are plucked up. For the proclamation of salvation must prevail. "The Gospel must be preached in the whole world." "Every tongue must confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father." Since these things must certainly come to pass, the unbelief that now prevails among some is not of the Father's planting. It belongs to the one who sows weeds among the wheat, or who plants the vine of Sodom beside the Lord's vineyard. So what we were taught by the Lord's voice in the Gospel, we have now been taught also in the riddle of Ecclesiastes: the same moment is the time both to receive the saving plant of faith and to pluck up the weed of unbelief. And what has been said about one particular achievement, faith, may consistently be applied to every virtue. There is a time to plant self-control and to pluck up the plant of licentiousness. So too, when justice is planted, the shoot of injustice is uprooted; the plant of humility overturns pride; and love, as it sprouts, withers the evil tree of hatred. Just so, conversely, from the opposite tree, that of hatred, [?] "lawlessness, multiplying, made love grow cold." And so on with everything else in the same way. We need not linger over each one; if we understand them all in the same manner, we shall not go wrong. Again, the next saying agrees with what we have already examined. "A time," he says, "to kill, a time to heal." This is clearly explained beforehand in the prophetic word, which says in the person of God, "I will kill, and I will make alive." For unless we kill the enmity within ourselves, we shall not heal the loving disposition in us that has fallen sick through hatred. So too with everything else that lives within us to our harm. I mean the evil battle line of the passions, this civil war that campaigns against us through pleasures and takes us captive to the law of sin: there is a time to kill these. For the slaying of such things becomes the healing [?] of what has been weakened by sin. Physicians say that worms and certain other such creatures are bred inside the intestines from bad humors, and that their life becomes the body's sickness. But if they are destroyed by some medicinal draught, the sick person will recover his health. These bodily afflictions correspond to the diseases of the soul. When anger drains us from within, or saps the soul's vigor and its thoughts through resentment, or when the beast of envy, or some other evil of the kind, is bred by a bad regimen, the one who perceives that his soul is nourishing a beast within will make timely use of the remedy that destroys the passions. This remedy is the teaching of the Gospel, so that once those creatures are slain, healing comes to the one who has done it. "A time to pull down, and a time to build up." This too can be learned from what was said by

God to the prophet Jeremiah, who was given power from God first to pull down, root out, and dig up, and then to set up, build, and plant. For the edifices of wickedness within us must first be demolished; then we find the time and the room to construct the temple of God, which is built in souls and whose material is virtue. For if anyone builds on this foundation gold or silver or precious stones, these are called virtue; while wood, hay, and straw signify the nature of vice, which is fit for nothing but to be burned up. So when the buildings are of hay and straw, that is, of injustice and arrogance and the rest of life's wickedness, the word bids us first to destroy these, and then to make the gold of virtue the material for building the spiritual house. For silver cannot grow together with straw, nor gold be fastened to hay, nor a pearl to wood. If the one is to exist, the other must be done away with entirely. For what fellowship has light with darkness? So the things of darkness will be pulled down first, and then the shining buildings of life will be constructed. "A time to weep, and a time to laugh." This saying is made clear by the voice of the Gospel spoken in the person of the Lord, which says, "Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted." Now, then, is the time to weep, while the time to laugh is laid up in hope; for present dejection will become the mother of the joy we hope for. Who would not spend his whole life in lamentation and gloom, if he became aware of himself and recognized what he had and what he lost, and in what state nature was at the beginning and in what state it is now? Then there was no death, and disease was absent. "Mine" and "yours," those wicked words, were at first banished from life. For as the sun is common, and the air is common, and above all God's grace is common and his blessing common, so in equal measure the sharing of every good lay open to all freely. The disease of greed was unknown, and those who had less felt no hatred toward those above them. For there was no superiority at all. And there were countless other things besides, which no one could even express in words, far surpassing in grandeur those already mentioned. I mean equal honor with the angels, freedom of speech before God, the contemplation of goods beyond the world, and our being adorned with the ineffable beauty of the blessed nature, displaying in ourselves the divine image shining forth [?] with the beauty of the soul. But in place of these, what an evil swarm of passions, what a wicked wasps' nest of sorrows! Which of life's evils should one name first? All are on a par with one another, all excel in the extremity of their evil, all give equal cause for lament. For which part of our misery would one lament most? From what point would one rather begin to bewail our nature: the brevity of

life, its toil, the way it begins with tears and ends in tears, pitiable infancy, the dotage of old age, the instability of youth, the heavy labors of those in their prime, the burden of marriage, the loneliness of the unmarried, the rootlessness of the childless, the envy that wealth attracts, the pain of poverty? I say nothing of the many kinds of disease, the mutilations, the amputations, the putrefactions, the loss of the senses, the derangements caused by demons, all that nature contains within itself, since every human being potentially carries these afflictions in his nature. I pass over the madness of erotic passion and the foul mire in which such frenzy ends. Nor do I mention the disgust that attaches to food through its excretion, lest I seem to be denouncing life in every respect and showing our nature to be a kind of dung-maker. Leaving all these and the like aside, I say that what is most worthy of tears, for those who perceive it, is this: we all know that when this shadowy life has run its course, there awaits us a certain expectation of judgment and a fury of fire that will devour the adversaries. Will not the one who reckons with these and similar things live always in lament? So now would be the time to take these things to heart. For if we are gloomy toward the present life, it will naturally follow that we commit no fault in it. And when this is achieved, the promised grace of joy will be laid up for us in hope; and hope does not put to shame, as the Apostle says. What follows is a kind of repetition of what was said before. For after speaking of the right time for tears and laughter, he added: "A time to beat the breast, a time to dance," which is nothing other than an intensification of each of the two already mentioned. For a deep and heartfelt lament is what Scripture calls beating the breast. Likewise dancing signifies the intensification of joy, as we have learned in the Gospel, where it says, "We piped for you, and you did not dance; we lamented for you, and you did not beat your breasts." So the history tells us that the Israelites beat their breasts at the departure of Moses, and that David danced as he led the procession of the ark when he brought it back from the foreigners, not appearing in his usual manner. For it says that he sang along to harmonious melodies as he struck up on his musical instrument, moved his feet in time with the rhythm, and by the rhythmic movement of his body made public his inner disposition. Since, then, man is twofold, made of soul and body, and life too is twofold, corresponding to each of the parts at work in us, it would be good, while we beat our breasts in the bodily life (and this life offers many occasions for lament), to prepare a harmonious dance for the soul. For the more life is darkened by dejection, the more

the occasions of joy are gathered up for the soul. Self-control is gloomy; humility is downcast; suffering loss is cause for lament; not having an equal share with the powerful is cause for grief. But he who humbles himself will be exalted, and he who struggles against poverty will be crowned, and he who is covered with sores and shows his life in every way worthy of lament will rest in the bosom of the Patriarch. May we too come to be there, by the mercy of our Savior Jesus Christ, to whom be the glory and the power to the ages of ages.

"A time to cast stones, and a time to gather stones." By what he has already shown, the commander of the Church's forces has increased the strength of his hearers, so that they can both strike their opponents and supply themselves with what they need for throwing. For what we were taught before, from which we learned to fit the measure of time to all things and to make timeliness in everything the test of the good, leads us to this power. We may conceive of a kind of arm of the soul, which hurls at the target the stones that destroy the enemy, and then calls back whatever stones we have cast at the foe, so that it may always strike down the adversary with the same ones. Those who look only to the letter and settle for the obvious sense of the words will perhaps apply the law of Moses to the present text, since the law commands that stones be thrown at anyone found transgressing. This we have learned from the history itself, in the cases of those who sinned against the Sabbath, of the man who stole sacred things, and of the other offenses for which the law prescribed the penalty of stoning. As for me, if Ecclesiastes had not also declared it timely to gather stones (something no law commands and no deed in the history parallels), I would have agreed with those who interpret the saying by the law, taking the time to cast stones to be when someone violates the Sabbath or steals something consecrated. But as it is, the further statement that the stones must be gathered again, which no law lays down, leads us to another meaning. Let us learn what kind of stones these are, which, after being thrown, must again become the property of the one who threw them. For when we cast stones in due time, we are taught to gather them again in due time. Indeed, it seems to me that not even the law should be taken so baldly [?], in its obvious sense. For what is great and worthy of God appears in the bare sense of what is written? If someone was caught gathering sticks on the Sabbath, did the man have to be stoned for that, when no injustice appears in the offense? Whom did he wrong by twigs that happened to be scattered about the wilderness, for the needs of a fire,

when he gathered them? He is not accused of taking what belonged to another, which would make it reasonable to think that an injustice was being punished. Rather, what lay open to all in common becomes for him the cause of his stoning. It is because he did this on the Sabbath that he is condemned as a wrongdoer. Who does not know that each thing done is judged by its own nature, whether it is evil or not? The time in which an action is performed is considered apart from the nature of the deed. For what does a span of time have to do with what we accomplish by our own choice? If someone asks us what a day is, we will surely answer that it is the sun's being above the earth, and we make dawn and evening its limits. But this definition of a day will not apply to only one of the days that recur in the weekly cycle. For the first, the second, and so on to the seventh, the definition is the same, and the Sabbath day differs in no way from the others in being a day. And if one examines what sin means, we will surely say it is the principle that one must do nothing against one's neighbor: for instance, "You shall not commit adultery, you shall not murder, you shall not steal," and the rest. There is a general law that contains each of these particulars within itself, namely the command to love one's neighbor as oneself. These things, whether kept or transgressed, are equally so on every day: they are either wholly good or understood as the opposite. No one would think that what was judged evil when done today, whether the offense was murder or anything else forbidden, would be good on the following day. If, then, evil is always evil, at whatever time someone dares to do it, so too what is blameless would not become blameworthy because of the time. If, then, gathering sticks and lighting a fire before the Sabbath is free of wrongdoing and punishment, how does this same act become an offense on the following day? But I know the Sabbath of rest; I know the law of inactivity, which commands man to be inactive without having fettered his natural activity. For it would indeed be commanding the impossible if it ordered us to be inactive, since for us, apart from all other works, the very form of life is a work: seeing for the eyes, the natural activity of hearing, smelling for the nostrils, drawing in air for the mouth, speech for the tongue, the handling of food for the teeth, digestion for the bowels, movement for the feet, and for the hands whatever these members are naturally made to do. How then can the law of inactivity be enforced on those whose nature does not admit of idleness? How shall I persuade the eye not to see on the Sabbath, when its nature is always to be seeing something? How shall I check the activity of hearing? How shall my sense of smell be persuaded to lay aside its perception of odors on the Sabbath? How shall the bowels refrain from their own function in obedience to the law, so that food remains undigested in the body, in order to show nature idle on the Sabbath? If, then, the rest of our body cannot accept the law of idleness (for nothing at all in life will be without activity), it is altogether impossible that the

…Sabbath, even if the hand or the foot stays motionless in the same posture and place. The law is laid down not for some one part of a person but for the whole person. So we shall not keep the law any better by keeping one of our limbs idle if we break the commandment by using our other senses as nature directs. Yet the law certainly comes from God, and nothing God commands is, so to speak, contrary to nature or shown to lie outside the principle of virtue. Idleness without reason is not virtue. We must therefore ask what the precept of Sabbath rest means. I say, then, that all the legislation given by God has a single aim: that those who have received the law should be clean of the work of evil. Every law that forbids what is prohibited commands us to keep Sabbath from evil works. This is the meaning of the tablets, of the Levitical observance and of the strictness of Deuteronomy: that we should be idle and inactive in those things whose work is evil. If someone understands the law in this way, that a person is to be idle in evil, then I too agree with the wise Ecclesiastes when he fixes a time for throwing stones at the man who gathers wood for himself. By this the gathering of the kindling of evil, collected as fuel for fire, is prevented. But if the letter is left bare, I do not know how anyone could find in the law what is worthy of God. We must therefore understand what the stones are that are thrown at such a man, so that his zeal for gathering kindling may not reach its goal. As for the wood with which the fire will be lit for the man who gathered it, its meaning is surely not obscure to anyone who brings even some mystical interpretation to the text. The Apostle rightly calls evil building 'wood, hay and straw,' because such buildings become fire at the time of judgment. The voice of the Gospel says that the chaff is made ready for fire, and it declared the fruitless branch fit only for the fire. So it would be clear that the wood gathered in preparation for fire is the vain pursuits of life. And whoever takes the man stoned at the proper time to be the thought that leans toward evil would not miss the mark. We must certainly understand that the thoughts that destroy evil are the stones that Ecclesiastes slings with good aim,

…so excellent that it both slays the enemy and never leaves the hand of the one who throws it. Whoever strikes down the licentious thought with the stone of self-control, the thought that gathers the fuel of fire through pleasures, both defeats it with the throw and always carries the weapon in his hand. In the same way justice becomes a stone against injustice: it destroys injustice and is kept in the bosom of the one who hurled it. Likewise, everything understood as belonging to the better destroys the worse and is never separated from the one who achieves virtue. And on our interpretation we must throw the stones at the right time and gather stones at the right time in such a way that we always send forth good shots to destroy what is worse, and never let our abundance of such weapons run short. The saying that comes next in order [concerns] the right time and the wrong time for a certain embrace…

The text runs as follows: 'A time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing.' These meanings could not become clear to us in any other way unless we first understand the expression through Scripture, so that we see in what sense the inspired word is accustomed to use the term. The great David indicated it in the Psalms when he cried out: 'Encircle Zion and embrace her.' And this same Solomon, when he was describing the inward union of one who is lovingly disposed toward wisdom, speaks of the other things through which we are joined to virtue and then adds this: 'Honor her, that she may embrace you.' David, then, bids us embrace Zion, and Solomon said that those who honor wisdom are embraced by her. So perhaps we shall not miss the fitting sense once we learn what it is that is timely to embrace. Zion is a mountain that rises above the citadel of Jerusalem. The one who urges you to embrace it is therefore bidding you grow together with the lofty way of life, so as to reach the very citadel of the virtues, which he indicates in a riddle by the name Zion. And the one who makes you dwell with wisdom brings you the good news of the embrace that follows from it. So it is a time to embrace Zion and to be embraced by wisdom. The name Zion points to the loftiness of the way of life, while wisdom, a part of virtue, signifies the whole of virtue. If we have learned from what has been said when it is the right time to embrace, the same passages have taught us from what things it is more profitable to be separated. For there is 'a time,' it says, 'to refrain from embracing.' Whoever has become intimate with virtue has become a stranger to his attachment to evil. 'For what fellowship has light with darkness, or Christ with Belial?' How can someone who serves two opposing masters be loyal to both? Love for the one has produced hatred of the other. So when the disposition of love secures the good, and this is the right time,

estrangement from its opposite truly follows. If you have truly loved self-control, you will have hated its opposite. If you look on purity with love, you have clearly loathed the stench of the mire. If you have cleaved to the good, you have surely been far removed from cleaving to the evil. And if someone should also apply the sense of 'embracing' to embracing wealth, this saying too shows what kind of wealth it is good to embrace, and what possessions we should refuse to embrace. I know a treasure that is eagerly sought: the one hidden in the field, not the one that is visible to all. I also know a wealth that is held in dishonor: not the wealth we hope for, but the one that appears before our eyes. The voice of the Apostle teaches this when it says: 'We look not at the things that are seen but at the things that are not seen; for the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal.' If we have understood this, we shall also have understood the next saying through it. 'For there is a time,' it says, 'to seek, and a time to lose.' Whoever has understood from what we have examined what he should keep away from embracing and what he should be joined to will know both what he ought to seek and what things it is a gain to lose. 'For there is a time,' it says, 'to seek, and a time to lose.' What, then, must I seek in order to hit upon the proper time? Prophecy shows what ought to be sought when it says: 'Seek the Lord and be strengthened,' and again: 'Seek the Lord, and when you find him, call upon him; and let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice.' Through these words, then, I have learned what one must seek: that whose finding is the very act of always seeking. For seeking is not one thing and finding another; the gain of seeking is the seeking itself. Do you also wish to learn the right time, when it is time to seek the Lord? I say it briefly: the whole of life. For in this matter alone the right time for zeal is all zeal [?]. Seeking the Lord is not good at some appointed time or fixed period. Never ceasing at all, but always seeking: this is the true right time. 'My eyes,' it says, 'are ever toward the Lord.' Do you see how carefully the eye searches for what it seeks, allowing itself no rest and no pause in contemplating the object of its search? By adding the word 'ever' he showed that the zeal is continual and unceasing. Let us understand the time to lose in the same way, judging it a gain to lose anything whose possession is a loss to the one who has it. Avarice is a bad possession, so let us lose it. Resentment is an evil hoard, so let us throw it away. Licentious desire is a ruinous possession; above all others let us be poor in this one, so that through such poverty we may gain the kingdom. For 'blessed are the poor in spirit,' clearly meaning those who [are rid?] of such wealth [?]

…and of all the other treasures of the devil. It is more blessed never to have acquired any of them in the first place, so that we may be entirely without possessions that defile. But it is no less good for someone who has been caught by this evil acquisition to lose such possessions and bring them to nothing. Never to have had any share in such things at all is beyond human nature, but human power is able to destroy them once they have been acquired. Therefore to have held none of the adversary's possessions belongs to the Lord alone, who shared our sufferings without sin. 'For the ruler of this world is coming,' he says, 'and finds nothing of his own in me.' But cleansing oneself through diligent repentance can be seen even among people who make themselves shine through virtue. Paul lost the evil possession of unbelief; through the grace of prophecy working in him he became full of the treasure he had sought. In the cleansing by the divine coal Isaiah lost all filth, both of word and of thought, and so he was filled with the Holy Spirit. In taking a share of the better, anyone loses everything understood as its opposite. So the temperate man loses licentiousness, the just man injustice, the modest man arrogance, the kindly man envy, the loving man enmity. The blind man in the Gospel found what he did not have by losing what he had: when his blindness was taken away, the radiance of light entered in its place. With the leper, when the disease vanished, the grace of health returned. With those raised from death, deadness gave way at the presence of life. In the same way, in the philosophy set before us it is impossible to acquire any of the lofty things unless we lose our zeal for earthly and lowly things. In finding these, we lose the more precious things; and conversely, the loss of these will bring about the finding of what is precious. We have learned this from the voice of the Lord: 'Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it.' When the soul is found among material pursuits, this causes it not to be found among the true goods; and conversely, being deprived of these and losing them becomes possession of the things hoped for. 'For what does a man profit if he gains the whole world but forfeits his soul?' 'A time,' it says, 'to seek, and a time to lose.' If, then, we have learned what the gain is that we seek, the gain found by losing what was wrongly acquired, let us seek the one and lose the other: let us seek what is good and lose what is evil. The next words of the text follow well and fittingly on what we have examined. It says: 'A time to keep, and a time to cast away.' Keep what? Clearly what we have found by seeking. Cast away what? Surely whatever we judged it profitable to lose. A thought came to you

that was upright. A desire to see God entered you; your soul thirsted for God, the mighty, the living; a longing came upon you to be in the courts of the Lord. In my view the courts of the Lord would be the virtues, in which the Word dwells, together with everyone who follows the Word. Keep these, so that the wealth of the pure possessions of your mind may not slip away from you. Some opposing thought creeps in like a secret thief, bent on destroying pure thoughts. It must be cast out and banished from the mind. By driving it away we shall keep our treasure of good things safe. But if the destroyer is not cast out, the possession will bring no gain, since its riches drain away through the schemes of burglars. We have been taught the time to seek, and 'everyone who seeks finds.' So, in order that what we have found may remain, let us set a careful guard over the treasure. 'With all vigilance,' it says, 'keep your heart': after finding, we must keep the grace we have found, such as the [grace?] [?] that someone who came in faith found through the washing. But it is harder work to keep what one has received than to find what one did not have. We said that the right time for seeking is not limited to some period, but that the whole of life is one single time for that good seeking. In the same way we declare that the time for keeping is measured by the whole of life, and we cite again now the same voice of prophecy, which says: 'My eyes are ever toward the Lord, for he will pluck my feet out of the snare.' The safe keeping of our good possession lies in this: in making God the guardian of what is ours. For when my eyes are ever toward the Lord, the snares of the adversary become useless, the snares by which he contrives his plots against the precious things in the soul. 'Do not let your foot be moved,' it says, 'and he who keeps you will not slumber.' So the present saying follows from the one before it. That one bade us seek so that we might find; this one advises us to keep, so that we may not lose. And the way to keep good things is to cast out whatever is understood as their opposite. In a city at war the garrison becomes more secure once the traitors have been driven out; as long as they remain inside, those hidden enemies plot more harm than the open ones. For 'a time,' it says, 'to keep, and a time to cast away.' The next part of the text leads the soul to a higher philosophy about intelligible things. It shows that the universe is continuous with itself and that the harmony of intelligible things has no break; instead, beings share a kind of concord with one another. The universe is not cut off from its connection with itself; rather, all things remain in being because they are held together by the power of Being. And true Being is either goodness itself

or whatever name above this one might conceive to signify the incorruptible nature. But how could anyone find a name for that which, as the divine voice of the Apostle says, is above every name? Yet whatever name may be found to interpret that inexpressible power and nature, what it signifies is surely good. This good, or what is above the good, truly exists in itself, and through itself it has given and still gives to beings both the power to come into being and continuance in being. Everything considered as outside it is non-existence, for what is outside Being does not have being. Evil is regarded as the opposite of love, and God is perfect virtue. Evil, therefore, is outside God, and its nature is grasped not in its being something but in its not being good. For we have given the name evil to what lies outside the notion of the good. So evil is set against the good as non-being is distinguished from being. By the free choice of our impulse we flowed away from the good. Those who are not in light are said to see darkness, for seeing darkness is simply seeing nothing. In the same way, the nature of evil, which has no existence, then took on substance in those who had flowed away from the good, and it exists only as long as we remain outside the good. But if the free movement of our will should break away again from its attachment to the non-existent and grow together with Being, then evil, no longer having being in me, will not have existence at all. For evil does not exist lying by itself apart from free choice. And I, having fastened and sewn myself to true Being, remain in Being, which always was, will be forever, and now is. These, it seems to me, are the thoughts suggested by 'a time to tear and a time to sew': that we should be torn away from what we wrongly grew together with, and be joined to that which it is good to be joined to. 'For it is good for me,' it says, 'to cleave to God, to put my hope in the Lord.' One might also apply this counsel profitably to many other things, for example: 'Drive out the wicked person from among you.' The divine Apostle gives this command concerning the man condemned for unlawful intercourse, ordering him to be torn away from the common fullness of the Church, 'so that,' he says, the small leaven of the condemned man's wickedness may not spoil the whole lump of the church's prayer. But through repentance he joins again the one who was torn away through sin, saying: 'so that such a person may not be swallowed up by excessive sorrow.' Thus he knows how to tear off the stained part of the Church's tunic at the right time, and to sew it back on at the right time, once it has been washed clean of its defilement through repentance. Many such things can be seen both in the older narratives and in our own day, in what is carried out by wise management in the Churches. For you know what we are torn away from and what we are always sewn to. Splitting away from heresy, we are always sewn into piety. And we see the Church's tunic whole and untorn when it has been torn away from communion

with heresy. But whether the text is philosophizing about beings according to the interpretation we examined earlier, or teaching such lessons through this counsel, the saying is in every respect beneficial and useful. At the right time it tears away things whose connection is evil, and at the right time it joins again things whose union is beneficial. Let us now go on to the next part of the text, where, it seems to me, the interpretation based on the higher philosophy fits the wording more closely. For the time to keep silence is placed first, and after silence the text has given the time to speak. When, then, and about what, is it better to be silent? Someone who looks to moral conduct might say that in many cases silence is more seemly than speech. Paul, for example, distinguishes the right time for silence from the right time for speech, sometimes laying down silence as a law and sometimes permitting speech: 'Let no rotten word come out of your mouth.' This is the law of silence. 'But if there is a good word for building up the faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear': this is the time for speaking. 'Let the women keep silence in the churches': again he has given silence its time. 'But if they wish to learn anything they do not know, let them ask their own husbands at home': again he has shown the right time for speech. 'Do not lie to one another': this too is a right time for silence. 'Let each one speak the truth with his neighbor': again, permission to speak. Many such examples can also be cited from the older Scripture: 'When the sinner stood against me, I was struck dumb and humbled, and I kept silent from good things'; and 'like a deaf man I did not hear, and like a mute who does not open his mouth.' The one who stays unmoved and does not repay evil becomes voiceless. But where it is right to use speech, he opens his mouth in parables, utters riddles, fills his mouth with praise and makes his tongue a pen. But since there are countless examples in Scripture, why should we labor over points that everyone accepts?
