Instead I wish to return to what came into my mind earlier, since the right time for silence and speech agrees with the interpretation given of tearing and sewing, and to state it briefly. In that passage the text tore away the soul that had wrongly grown onto the opposite, and through cleaving led it into union with true Being, which is beyond words, as the preceding discussion explained. Here, it seems to me, silence is placed first for this reason: what is above every thought and name, what the soul torn away from evil always seeks and, once it has found it, longs to be sewn to, is [beyond] every voice that tries to interpret it…

is higher. Whoever insists on dragging it down to what a word can signify unwittingly offends against the Divine. For what is believed to be above everything must certainly be above speech as well. But whoever tries to grasp the unbounded in words no longer allows that the thing he is presenting is above everything. He supposes it to be of such a kind and of such a size as his own words were able to express. He does not know that a conception of the one who truly is, worthy of God, is kept only by being persuaded that the Divine is beyond knowledge. For everything that exists in creation looks toward what is akin to it by nature, and nothing that exists remains in being once it has gone outside itself. Fire does not stay in water, nor water in fire; the land creature does not live in the deep, nor the water creature on dry land; the earthbound creature does not live in the air, nor again the creature of the air in the earth. Each thing exists only so long as it stays within the proper bounds of its nature. If it goes outside itself, it will also go outside existence. The power of the senses works the same way: it keeps to its natural activities and cannot cross over to the sense beside it. The eye does not do the work of hearing, hearing does not taste, touch does not speak, and the tongue does not do the work of sight or of hearing; each has its own natural activity as the limit of its power. In the same way, the whole of creation cannot go outside itself by means of comprehending contemplation. It always remains within itself, and whatever it sees, it sees itself. Even if it should think it sees something above itself, it has no power by nature to see what lies outside itself. For example, in contemplating the things that exist, it strains to pass beyond the notion of extension, but it does not get past it. With every concept it finds, it always perceives along with it the extension that is grasped together with the existence of the thing conceived, and extension is nothing other than creation. But that good which we have learned to seek and to keep, being above creation, is above comprehension. Our mind travels through extended duration. How then could it grasp the nature that has no extension, when, by working its way back through time, it is always searching out what is older than the things it finds? It has run through everything that can be known by busy inquiry, but it finds no device by which to run past the notion of the age itself, so as to set itself outside itself and rise above that which is seen before all existing things, and above the age itself. Instead it is like someone who finds himself on a mountain ridge. Let us imagine a smooth and sheer rock, rising upright from below, stretching down to an endless depth, and at the top holding up that summit whose overhanging brow drops away into a gaping abyss. Think what a person is likely to feel when the tip of his foot touches the edge of the ridge leaning over the depth, and he finds no footing for his foot and no handhold for his hand. That, it seems to me, is what the soul experiences when it has passed beyond the firm ground of extended things and searches for the nature that is before the ages and without extension. It has nothing to take hold of: no place, no time, no measure, nothing else of that kind. That nature does not allow our mind to set foot on it. Slipping on every side from what cannot be grasped, the soul grows

dizzy and helpless, and turns back again to what is akin to it. It is content to know only this much about what lies above: to be persuaded that it is something other than the nature of the things that are known. That is why, when speech reaches the things that are beyond speech, it is the time to keep silent, and to hold the wonder of that unspeakable power, uninterpreted, in the secret places of the conscience. We know that even the great ones spoke of the works of God, and not of God himself, saying: "Who shall tell of the mighty acts of the Lord?" and "I will recount all your works," and "Generation after generation shall praise your works." These they speak of and describe in detail, and they entrust the telling of what has been done to the voice. But when speech concerns the one who stands above every thought, they plainly lay down silence by what they say. For they say that of the magnificence of the glory of his holiness there is no end. What a wonder! How the word feared to approach the glory of the divine wonder, so that it could not grasp the wonder even of one of the things seen from outside! It did not say that the essence of God has no end, since it judged it altogether rash even to take this into one's thought. Instead, its words marvel at the magnificence that is seen upon the glory. Yet it could not see the essence even of the glory itself; it was struck with amazement on perceiving the glory of his holiness. How far, then, he kept from prying into the nature as it is, when he did not have the strength to marvel even at the furthest of the things that appear before it! He did not marvel at his holiness, nor at the glory of the holiness. He set out to marvel only at the magnificence of the glory of the holiness, and even in the wonder of that he failed, for his mind did not grasp the limit of what he marveled at. That is why he says: "Of the glory, of the magnificence, of his holiness there is no end." So in our speech about God, when the inquiry concerns his essence, it is the time to keep silent. But when it concerns some good activity of his, the knowledge of which comes down even to us, then it is time to tell of his mighty acts, to proclaim his wonders, to recount his works, and to use speech up to that point. In what lies beyond, we should not permit creation to step outside its own bounds, but should be content if it knows itself. For if, as our argument shows, creation does not yet know itself, has not yet grasped what the essence of the soul is, or the nature of the body, where existing things come from, how they come into being from one another, how what is not is brought into being, how what is dissolves into what is not, what this harmony of opposites in the world is—if creation does not know itself, how will it describe what is above itself? It is therefore the time to keep silent about these things, for in them silence is better. But it is the time to speak of the things by which our life advances toward virtue, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be the glory and the power to the ages of ages. Amen.

Chapter 3, verse 8: "A time to love, and a time to hate." Who will have ears so purified that he can receive purely what is said about loving, bringing with him nothing of filthy love? Perhaps our ears too need the fingers of Jesus, so that by the divine touch of the true Word the hearing power of our soul may be set free from every filth that stops up the hearing. Then we may understand the love that is praiseworthy, and take into our soul what the time to love is and what the time to hate is. I think this time is nothing other than the time of what is beneficial. In my judgment, the benefit that comes from each of these lies in using both at the right moment; so if anything is done outside what is profitable, what is done would also be outside the right time. But first, I think, we must understand what these two words mean, "to love" and "to hate," so that in this way our discussion may also grasp the timely use of them. Love is the inward disposition toward what is agreeable, brought into action through pleasure and attachment. Hatred is estrangement from what is unpleasant and a turning away from what causes pain. Each of these dispositions can be used profitably, and also in the opposite way; indeed, the whole life of virtue, so to speak, takes its beginning from here. For wherever we incline in love, that we make our own in our souls, and toward whatever we are disposed with hatred, from that we become estranged. Whether the soul's disposition is toward the good or toward evil, the thing loved is somehow blended with the soul. And wherever hatred comes in between, it brings about separation from that thing, whether it is the good or the worse. We must therefore examine what is by nature lovable and what is hateful, so that by using this disposition of the soul at the right time, we may become estranged from evil through hatred and be blended with the nature of the good. If only human nature were taught this before everything else—I mean, to distinguish the good from what is not good! The passions would have found no way into our life if we had known the good from the beginning. As it is, from the very first we make irrational sense-perception the judge of the good, and we grow up together with the judgment about things that forms in us at the start. For this reason we are hard to drag away from the things that sense has judged to be good, since we have built up our attachment to them by growing up with them. People think beautiful whatever gives the eyes some pleasure by its fine color, whether in lifeless

matter or in living sights. To the hearing, melody is beautiful; and among flavors and smells, taste defines one thing as good and smell another. But the heaviest and most irrational of all is touch, through which unbridled pleasure naturally takes the lead in voting on what is good. Since, then, the senses are born together with us as soon as we come into being, and we are brought up with them from the beginning of life; and since the sensory power is closely akin to irrational life (for all such things are seen in irrational animals as well); while the mind is somehow hindered from its proper activity, having no room in infancy, and is in a way squeezed out by the dominance of the more irrational sense—for this reason the misdirected and mistaken use of the loving disposition becomes the beginning and foundation of a life of vice. For since our nature is twofold, a blend of the intelligible and the sensible, our life is accordingly twofold as well, each kind arising in us in a corresponding way: bodily in the sensible part, and incorporeally in the other. In the same way, the good and what is not good are not the same for each form of our life. For the intelligible part, the good is intelligible; for the sensible and bodily part, it is whatever sense wants. Since sense, then, grows together with us from our first birth, while the mind waits for us to advance to a suitable age so that it can gradually show itself in the person, the mind, which develops little by little, is ruled by sense. It is forcibly accustomed to obey whatever is always stronger, judging good or bad whatever sense chooses or rejects. That is why a true understanding of what is really good becomes difficult and hard for us to achieve: we have been seized beforehand by the judgments of sense, defining the good as what delights and gives pleasure. Just as one cannot see the beauties of the sky when mist has taken hold of the air overhead, so the eye of the soul does not look upon virtue, since pleasure has covered its sight as with a fog. Since, then, sense looks toward pleasure, and the mind is hindered by pleasure from seeing virtue, this becomes the beginning of vice: the mind, ruled by sense, has also cast its vote for sense's irrational judgment about the good. If the eye says that the good lies in the fine color of what appears, the understanding too leans along with it. And in the other cases likewise, whatever delights the sense carries off the vote as the good. But if it had somehow been possible for the true judgment about the good to arise in us from the beginning, with the mind testing the good by itself, we would not be enslaved to irrational sense and reduced to the state of cattle. So that this confusion in us may be sorted out, and what is by nature lovable, and again what is otherwise, may be recognized without error, the Preacher now says in his discourse: "A time to love, and a time to hate." By this he distinguishes the nature of things, showing what is beneficial to love

and what to hate. Youth, boiling with the passions of its age, says that it is the time for it to love the things that youth holds dear. But the Preacher cries out against youth, marking out another time for pure love. For the soul's misguided attachment to unseemly things is not love at all. When nature is going well and healthy, thirst comes to the body at the proper time. But for those in whom the bite of the dipsas viper has produced this condition, no one would say that the thirst works at the proper time; in them thirst is not a natural appetite but a disease. In the same way, the filthy passion of youth is not love but a sickness, arising in an inclination inflamed by the bite of that age. So not every love is timely, but only the love directed toward what alone is lovable. We can gain clear knowledge about these things by dividing our discussion as follows. Of the goods that people pursue, some really are what they are called, while others bear the name falsely. Those that give no passing enjoyment, that are not good in one person's eyes and useless to others, but are always good, through everything, and in all in whom they come to be—these are truly good. They always remain the same and admit no mixture of the worse. To those who examine carefully, such things are seen only in the divine and eternal nature. All the other things that are good to the senses appear good through the deception of opinion. They neither are good by nature nor have real existence. They belong to a nature that flows and passes away, but through some deception and vain prejudice the uneducated suppose them to be real. So if people cling to unstable things and do not reach out for the things that always stand firm, the Preacher seems, as if standing on some high lookout, to cry out to human nature in the words "A time to love, and a time to hate," that the truly good things are different. They are beautiful in themselves and make those who share in them beautiful too. For whatever the nature of the thing shared, the one who shares in it must also be changed to match it. Thus the mouth becomes sweet-smelling when someone takes one of the fragrant spices into it, and foul-smelling again when someone eats garlic or something else with a stronger stench. All the filth of sin is foul-smelling, while virtue, on the contrary, is the fragrance of Christ; and a loving disposition naturally produces a blending with what is loved. So whatever we love passionately, that we become: either the fragrance of Christ or a stench. For whoever has loved the good will himself be good, since the goodness that comes to be in him

changes the one who received it into itself. That is why the one who always is sets himself before us as food: so that by taking him into ourselves we may become what he is. For he says, "My flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink." So whoever loves this flesh is not a lover of his own flesh, and whoever is devoted to this blood will be clean of the blood that belongs to the senses. For the flesh of the Word, and the blood contained in this flesh, have more than one grace: they are sweet to those who taste them, desirable to those who long for them, and lovely to those who love them. But if someone turns his love toward things that have no real existence, whatever those things are by nature, the one who has entered into them must certainly become like them. Since, then, among existing things some are true and others vain, [?] so that by setting them side by side we may understand the nature of what truly is. This is what all the saints do. They bring back those who have wandered from the straight road and are traveling on the wrong one, leading them to the road they turned from, and calling out from far off: "Flee the road you are on! There are robbers and thieves on it, and murderers lying in ambush." They do this so that the traveler may avoid the danger by turning off the deadly road, and his withdrawal from it may become guidance onto the road that saves. In the same way, the great Preacher cried out from on high to human nature, which was wandering, as the Prophet says, in a trackless place and not on a road, and his words plainly say this: "Why do you wander through life, O men? Why do you love vain things, and hold dear what has no substance, and cling with your affection to things that have no real existence? There is another road, one that does not lead astray and that saves. Love that one; travel on it through love. Its name is truth and life and incorruption and light and the like. But this road on which you are now running deserves hatred and aversion. It is without light and gripped by darkness, and it leads to cliffs and pits, to places full of wild beasts, and to the ambushes of robbers." So by saying "A time to love," he pointed out what is truly lovable and worthy of love; and by assigning a time to hatred, he taught what we must turn away from. Having learned, then, what is by nature lovable, let us embrace it with love, never turned aside by poor judgment about the good, spending our love on the very things that the great

my refuge and my deliverer." But about the opposite he says: "Whoever loves injustice hates his own soul. He will rain snares upon sinners." So the whole of our life is the time for love toward God, and our entire life is the time for estrangement from the adversary. Whoever spends even a small part of his life outside the love of God certainly comes to be outside the one from whose love he has separated himself. And whoever comes to be outside God must be outside the light, because God is light. He is outside life too, and incorruption, and every thought and thing that is seen to belong to what is better, since God is all these. For whoever is not in these is certainly in their opposites. So darkness and corruption, utter destruction and death await such a person. The Preacher's words distinguish these things in a brief phrase. They point them out through timely love and through hatred exercised at the right time, revealing the nature of each of the things understood as opposites. "There is a time," he says, "to love the good, and again a time to hate its opposite." And he says: "You, O man, should consider that the word looks toward the good." For the reversed and misguided disposition of our soul toward each of these is the root and beginning of sin. "No one," he says, "can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other." The contrast has taught us who rules wickedly, from whom we must be estranged through hatred, and who rules over his subject for good, to whom it is fitting to be joined through love. But if someone clings to what is hateful and despises what is lovable, he is the one who reverses the right times for love and hatred, to his own harm. For "whoever despises a thing will be destroyed by it," and whoever clings to destruction will win for himself the very thing he clung to. So if you distinguish in your reasoning the things understood as belonging to virtue and to vice, you will recognize the right time, and how you must stand toward each of them. Self-control and pleasure, temperance and licentiousness, modesty and conceit, goodwill and ill will, and all things understood as opposites, are plainly shown to you by the Preacher, so that by disposing your soul well toward them you may make profitable decisions. There is a time, then, to love self-control and to hate pleasure, so that you may not become a lover of pleasure but rather a lover of God. And the same holds for everything else: love of strife, love of gain, love of glory, and everything that, by turning love toward what it should not, cuts us off from our relationship with the good. From this we have learned in passing, as it were, a doctrine: that every movement of the soul was designed for good by the one who created our nature. But the mistaken use of such movements has given rise to the occasions for vice. Our power of free choice is something good, but when it is set to work toward evil it becomes the worst of evils. Conversely, the instrument of virtue is the

[?] …the power that repels what is unpleasant. Its name is hatred, when it is armed against what is opposed to us. But it becomes a weapon of sin when it is set in opposition to the good. So every creation of God among the things fashioned in us is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving. It is the ungrateful use of these things that has turned the creature into a passion, through which our kinship with God departs, and [?] contrary things are set up in God's place, so that for such people the passions are made into gods. Thus for gluttons the belly becomes a god. Thus the covetous make an idol of their disease. Thus those whose soul's eyes have been darkened by deceit in this age have made vainglory a god for themselves. To put it briefly, whatever a person yokes his own reason beneath, making it its slave and subject, he has made into a god in his own passion. He would not have suffered this unless he had made the evil his own through love. If, then, we have understood the right time both for love and for hatred, let us love the one and make war on the other. "For there is," it says, "a time for war and a time for peace." You see the battle line of the opposing passions, the law of the flesh that wars against the law of sin. Pay attention to the varied arrangement of the battle, and to how the enemy's strategy against your city comes from countless directions. He sends spies, wins over traitors, lies in wait along the roads, sets up ambushes and traps, recruits allies and builds siege engines. Slingers and archers, those who fight hand to hand, the cavalry and every such force he sends out against you. You surely know what these things mean: who the traitor is, who the spy, who the men in ambush, who the slingers, who the archers, who the close fighters and the squadron of horsemen. Since we see all this, we too must arm ourselves and call on allies. We must test those under our command to make sure none of them sides with the enemy. We must foresee the ambushes along the road and protect ourselves with shields against the missiles. We must [?] against those who engage us hand to hand from above [?], and cut off the approach of the horsemen who come against us with a trench. It would also be fitting to secure the walls with certain [?], so that they are not shaken by the siege engines. But there is surely no need of words to explain each point: how the enemy of each one's city, the city that God settled in the soul, tests our strength through spies, and has some of our own people who become traitors to our strength. To reveal the idea more clearly: the first assault of temptation, from which the passions take their beginning, is of this kind. It becomes the spy of our strength. For example, a sight has fallen on the eye that is able to rekindle desire. Through this, then, the enemy spies out the strength within you,

to see whether it is strong and well prepared, or slack and easily taken. If you did not bend before the form, and the tension of your mind was not loosened toward what appeared, but you let the encounter pass without passion, then you at once frightened off the spy. You showed him the readiness of your thoughts, like a phalanx of hoplites bristling with spears. But if the senses are softened by pleasure toward the sight, and the image of the form slips into the mind through the eyes, then the mind, the general of the forces within, is overcome, because it has nothing manly or vigorous but is sluggish and slack. And a crowd of traitors from the populace of the thoughts gathers around the spy. These are the traitors of whom the Lord says, "A man's enemies are those of his own household." They are the things that come out of the heart and defile the man, and their names can be learned clearly from the Gospel. From this point it should no longer be hard for you to understand, one after another, the details of that military array that lies in ambush unseen, into which those fall who walk the road of life without looking ahead. Those who, under the guise of friendship and goodwill, drag anyone who trusts them down to the ruin of sin are the ones lying in wait along the roads. They are the praisers of pleasure, those who lead people by the hand to the theaters, those who show how easy evil is and by their own conduct call others to imitate it, calling themselves brothers and friends to the ruin of those who perish. Of them it is written, "Every brother will utterly supplant, and every friend will walk in deceit." If we have understood the ambushes, it should also be clear how to search out the band of slingers, archers and javelin men. The insolent, the hot-tempered and the abusive start the insults. Instead of arrows or stones they shoot, sling and hurl provoking words, and they wound in the middle of the heart those who travel without breastplate or guard. And one would not go wrong in comparing the passion of conceit and arrogance to the prancing of horses. For some people are simply horses, stiff-necked and high-headed, who trample the modest with the swollen words of their conceit as if with hollow hooves. Of them Scripture says, "Let not the foot of pride come against me." As for the siege engines that break up the fitted structure of the wall, one might rightly take them to mean the love of money. For nothing in the enemy's equipment is so heavy and so hard to withstand as the engine of avarice. Even if the other virtues have been built around souls in a well-fitted construction, the engine still often breaks in, even through these. For one can see the love of money breaking in even through temperance and faith, through exactness about the mysteries, through self-control and humility, and getting inside all such things [?]

in this heavy and invincible assault of the [?]. That is why some who are self-controlled and temperate, fervent in faith, settled in their way of life and moderate in their habits, are unable to hold out against this one disease alone. If, then, we have understood the band of the enemy, it is time to make war. But no one would dare to rout the opposing battle line without taking hold of the Apostle's full armor. Surely no one is ignorant of the nature of that divine armor, by which he makes the one who stands against the enemy phalanx invulnerable to the enemy's arrows. The Apostle divides the virtues into kinds and makes each kind of virtue a weapon proper to each of our vital parts. He weaves and plaits righteousness together with faith, and from them he makes the soldier's breastplate, arming the soldier well and safely with both. For neither, separated from the other, can be a safe weapon in itself for the one who wields it. Faith without the works of righteousness is not enough to save, and righteousness of life, separated from faith, is not safe for salvation by itself either. That is why he weaves faith and righteousness together, as the materials of this weapon, and so protects the area around the soldier's heart, for the heart is understood to be within the breastplate. He protects the champion's head with hope, showing that the good soldier ought to have the hope of things on high as a kind of crest [?] pointing upward. The shield, the weapon that covers, is unbreakable faith, which the points of the darts cannot pierce. And by the darts the enemy shoots we should understand the varied assaults of the passions. The weapon of salvation that arms the right hand of those who fight bravely against the enemy is the Holy Spirit, fearsome to the adversary but saving to the one who wields it. And the whole teaching of the Gospel gives the feet their security, so that no part of the body is found bare and open to a blow. If, then, we have learned whom we must fight and how to take up the battle, we should also learn the other part: those with whom the word urges us to be at truce and at peace. Who, then, is the good general, to whom I may join myself through peace? And who is the king of such an army? Is it not clear, since we have heard both from the divinely inspired Scripture, that the heavenly army is the battle line of the angels? "There was," it says, "a multitude of the heavenly host praising God." Daniel sees ten thousand times ten thousand standing by, and beholds thousands upon thousands among those who minister. And the Prophet, bearing witness to this, calls the Lord of all "Lord of hosts" and "Lord of powers." And to the son of Nun the One mighty in war says, "I am the commander-in-chief

of the host." If we have understood what the good alliance is, and who leads these allies, let us make a treaty with him, let us run to his dominion, let us become friends of the one who holds such power. The way to become his own is taught to us by the one who brings this friendship together, the great Apostle, when he says, "Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God." And again: "We are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were making his appeal through us. We beg you on Christ's behalf: be reconciled to God." For as long as we were by nature children of wrath, doing what is not fitting, we were ranked among those who oppose the right hand of the Most High. [?] But once we have put away ungodliness and worldly desires, and live in holiness, righteousness and godliness, through this peace we shall be joined to the true Peace. For this is what the Apostle says of him: "He is our peace." This word is the end and the sum of all the things that are done in their time. For we were taught to do everything in its season so that we might achieve this for ourselves: to have peace with God by being set against the adversary as his enemy. And surely, even if someone were to call the virtues the army of peace, toward which we must be friendly, his account would not stray from the meaning given. For every name and idea of virtue refers back to the Lord of the virtues. But why prolong the discussion of such matters, when what has been said is enough to reveal the meaning contained in the words? But since through these things [?] the soul of one already trained in these lofty teachings, he again leads the soul of the one who follows the word up to a lofty state, and says, "What profit has the worker in that in which he toils?" This amounts to saying: What comes of all human toils, from which there is no gain? A man farms, sails the sea, endures hardship in the labors of soldiering, trades, suffers loss, makes a profit, goes to law, fights, goes away defeated, carries off the winning vote, is pitied, is called happy, stays at home, wanders in foreign lands: all the things seen in life in its various pursuits, some in one, others in another. What more does his zeal for these things bring to the one who spends his own life on them? Does not everything stop together with life and become covered by forgetfulness? Stripped of all he strove for, he departs naked, taking with him nothing of the affairs of this world except his own awareness of those affairs. And from this awareness, after this, a voice comes in a certain way [?] to the one who has wandered through life amid such occupations: What profit have you gained from all those many labors in which you toiled? Where are the splendid houses? Where are the buried purses? Where are the bronze statues, and the voices of those who acclaimed you? See, now there are fire and scourges, and

the incorruptible judgment, and the examination of the lives people have lived, which cannot be deceived. What profit, then, has the worker in that in which he toils? After this he says, "I have seen the distraction that he has given to the sons of men to be distracted by: all the things he made beautiful in their time. And indeed he has put the age in their heart, so that man may not find out the work that God has made from beginning to end." Why do you say this? "I have recognized," he says, "how human nature was distracted from life, taking its occasions from God's own benefits. He made all things for good, and he gave to those who share in existence a reason that can tell the better from the worse. When this reason recognizes the right time for using each thing, it grants those who use it the perception of what is good. But since human nature fell away from right judgment about things, and was turned aside from its settled reasoning by evil counsel, the changing of the right time turned what was useful in each case into the opposite experience." It is as if someone laid out on a table everything needed for a feast, and set beside it certain utensils suited to help with the food, such as craftsmen skilled in these things make: fine knives with which the guests cut themselves portions of what is set before them, or silver forks with a hollow formed at the other end that is made suitable for broth [?]. Then one of those invited to the feast reverses the use of the things provided and uses each one for what it should not be used for. With the knife he cuts either himself or one of those reclining beside him, and with the fork he gouges out his neighbor's eye or his own. One would say that this man misused the host's provision for evil. One would not say that the host himself had prepared the cause of what happened, but that the bad use of what was set out had brought the one who used it wrongly to this harm. "In the same way," he says, "I too have recognized that each thing came from God for every better purpose, provided that each is used in its season and as is fitting. But the perversion of right judgment about things has turned good things into an occasion for evils." I mean something like this: What is sweeter than the activity of the eyes? But when sight is overcome by passion and becomes the servant of such things, what was given as a benefit is said to have become a cause of evils. This means nothing other than that someone has used what is good badly and turned its use into a passion. So too with everything else that nature has from God: it depends on the choice of those who use it whether it becomes material for good or for evil. That is why he says, "All the things he made beautiful in their time," and "Indeed he has put the age in their heart." The age, being a notion of extension, signifies the whole creation that came to be within it. So the word points to everything contained by naming what contains it. All things, then, that came to be in the age God gave to the human heart for good, so that through the greatness and beauty of created things people might contemplate the one who made them. But they were harmed by the very things through which they had been benefited, because they did not use each one

as was proper and for their good. That is why he says, "so that man may not find out the work that God made" for the purpose of benefit in all the things that have come to be from the beginning of creation to the completion of the universe, since nothing among the things that exist is evil. For it is not in the nature of anything evil to spring from the good. And if the cause of all things is good, then surely everything that has its existence from the good is good.

Then he says, "I have recognized that there is no good in them except to rejoice and to do good in one's life." With these words he sums up what has been said. For if the use of God's works in their season defines what is good for human life, the one good would be continual rejoicing in good things, the joy that is born of good works. Keeping the commandments now gladdens the one who devotes himself to good works through hope. Afterward, once it has received the enjoyment of the good things hoped for, it sets before the worthy the joy that is their own, when the Lord says to those who have done good, "Come, you who are blessed, inherit the kingdom prepared for you." What food and drink are to the body, by which our nature is kept alive, looking toward the good is to the soul. And this is truly a gift of God: to gaze intently upon God. For this is the gift [?] that is explained in the words that follow. The passage runs as follows: "And indeed every man who eats and drinks [?]…" Just as a man gets his strength from eating and drinking, so one who looks toward something good (and the true good can only be the One who alone is good) has a gift of God in all his toil: this very thing, always looking toward the good. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power to the ages of ages. Amen.
